load"*. The crash report reads unlike every other one in this archive:

```
Stray-Win64-Shipping + 2f3ebd0     <- fault here
Stray-Win64-Shipping + 2b4f4f9
Stray-Win64-Shipping + 301ed32
Stray-Win64-Shipping + 1300c69
Stray-Win64-Shipping + 14627c5
segcap + 8759                       <- ProbeWorldState's lambda
segcap + 2485a                       <- ProcessEventDetour
```

Five **game** frames above ours. Everywhere else in this file, our code faults
and our frame is on top. Here the engine faults, and our frames are underneath
it — which is the signature of *we called in with something bad*, not *we read
something bad*.

I had already guessed wrong once about this crash. When it first appeared I
guarded `Engine::GetObject`, because the crash before it had been a torn read in
the object walk and this one came through the same probe. That fix was correct
in itself and did nothing here — the next run crashed at the identical address.
**Fixing the previous instance of a pattern is not the same as fixing this one.**

The actual cause is four lines up from the symbol:

```cpp
pe.RunOnGameThread([cdo, fp, fd, world](segcap::ue4::Engine&) {
```

`world` is captured **by value**, and `RunOnGameThread` *queues* the lambda — it
runs later, on the game thread. During a level transition the `UWorld` found a
moment earlier is destroyed before the callback arrives. We then pass that freed
pointer to `UGameplayStatics::IsGamePaused` as its `WorldContextObject`, and the
engine dereferences it.

No guard could have caught this. The pointer was perfectly readable; it had
simply stopped being a world. `IsReadable` answers "is this memory mapped", and
the question here is "is this still the object I think it is" — which is
unanswerable from the outside, and is the same distinction as §8.3, where address
identity stood in for object identity.

The fix is to resolve the world **inside** the callback instead of capturing it,
and it closes the window completely rather than narrowing it: UE tears levels
down on the game thread, and the callback runs on the game thread, so between the
lookup and the call the world cannot be destroyed — the thread that would destroy
it is the one executing our code.

The general form, and the reason this is worth more than the fix:

> **A pointer captured for later use on another thread is a fact with an expiry
> date that nothing in the type system records.** Queue the lookup, not the
> result.

And the diagnostic lesson: **when your frames are BELOW the fault rather than
above it, stop looking for a bad read and start looking for a bad argument.** I
spent two builds guarding reads because guarding reads had worked twice already.

## 9. What I would do differently

1. **Verify on the fixture before the game, always.** The one crash would have
   been caught in 12 seconds by the 3-buffer fixture I already had.
2. **Never let a probe filter its own evidence.** Absent and misread must be
   distinguishable, or the log answers a question you did not ask.
3. **Compare timestamps, not just facts.** §2.5 cost three runs because two log
   lines were read as independent rather than as a sequence.
4. **Check the arithmetic before adding a bound.** 3000 of 350,000 is 4%, and I
   shipped it as a robustness improvement. Same error in §7.5: 255 slots against
   38,000 primitives was never going to work by cycling.
5. **Diagnose my instrument before diagnosing someone's machine.** §7.1 is the
   worst instance in the project: the same symptom, misdiagnosed twice by
   inference, settled in one command once I actually asked the OS what the input
   desktop was called.
6. **Distinguish "absent" from "filtered".** §2.4 and §7.3 are the same bug two
   months apart. Any filter that can hide evidence needs a log line upstream of
   itself, or its silence is unreadable.
7. **Ask what the metric would look like if it were wrong.** `marked 250 this
   batch`, `255 live slots, 0 evictions`, and `21 masks captured` were all true
   and all describing failures. A counter that only goes up measures effort, not
   result — pair it with one that can go down.
8. **The engine usually already knows.** `WasRecentlyRendered` was in the
   reflected function list from the first successful discovery run. I spent a
   run building a slot lottery before reading the list I had already printed.
9. **Re-audit shared state when you add a thread, not when it crashes.** §7.11
   was unsafe from the first commit and invisible because only one thread wrote
   it. Adding a writer is the moment to re-read every global the new thread can
   reach — that review takes minutes, and the crash cost a full run plus the
   diagnosis.
10. **A handle is not an identity, in any layer.** §8.3 is the same bug as the
    UObject generational handle, one layer down. I wrote that guard, understood
    exactly why GC slot reuse breaks a stored pointer, and never asked whether
    the graphics API recycled handles the same way. When you fix a class of bug
    in one layer, go and ask the question in every other layer that stores a raw
    handle — that sweep costs an hour and this one cost four wrong diagnoses.
11. **Print the object, not your model of it.** Four hypotheses died the instant
    one log line showed the elected resource's real `GetDesc` next to what the
    election believed. Every diagnostic before it described my own bookkeeping
    back to me, so all of them agreed with each other and none of them agreed
    with the GPU.
```

`docs/FORMAT.md`:

```md
# Output format

A capture session produces, for every captured frame:

| file | contents |
|---|---|
| `segcap_mask_<N>.pgm` | 8-bit per-pixel object ids, binary PGM (P5) |
| `segcap_frame_<N>.ppm` | the rendered frame, binary PPM (P6), RGB24 |
| `segcap_mask_<N>.json` | the slot → object table for that frame |

and once per session:

| file | contents |
|---|---|
| `segcap_input.jsonl` | every controller state delivered to the game, timestamped |

## Actions, for world models

A world model learns `P(next frame | frame, action)`. A video without the actions
that produced it is half a training pair, so the input is recorded alongside the
frames.

The unusual property here is that the pipeline **synthesises** the input, so the
action is known exactly rather than inferred. There is no hook into the game's
input handling, no guessing at deadzone curves, no sampling race against the
game's polling. Each record is literally the report handed to the virtual pad
driver, written at the moment it was sent:

```json
{"t":1786260344126,"lx":0,"ly":24000,"rx":9000,"ry":0,"lt":0,"rt":0,"buttons":4096}
```

`buttons` is the XUSB bitfield (`0x1000` = A). Sticks are the native
−32768..32767; triggers 0..255.

**Joining frames to actions.** Every sidecar carries `timestampMs`, stamped at
`Present` — not when the readback lands, which is several frames later and would
shift every action label. `segcap_input.jsonl` uses the same clock. Both come
from `GetSystemTimeAsFileTime`, deliberately a wall clock rather than
`QueryPerformanceCounter`: the two logs are written by *different processes*
(the injected DLL and `vpad.exe`), so anything process-relative cannot be joined
across that boundary at all.

The join is a step function — the last sample at or before the frame — because
that is what a gamepad is. Interpolating between samples would invent stick
positions the game never saw. Frames further than 2s from any sample are
reported as having no known action rather than being attributed the nearest one.

The pad re-sends its held state at ~10Hz rather than only on change, so the log
has regular samples instead of one record per multi-second hold. Measured on a
300-frame session: **300/300 frames matched to an action.**

`tools/make_demo.py` draws this as a live controller panel under the video.

`<N>` is the same monotonic frame index in all three, so a mask and its frame
are paired by filename alone. They are the *same* frame by construction: both
are copied during the same `Present` call, so there is no synchronisation step
and nothing to drift.

## Why the sidecar is not optional

The stencil channel is 8 bits. Slot 42 in one frame and slot 42 in another can
be different objects, because 255 slots have to describe a level with ~33,000
markable primitives. The slot is a **lease**, not an identity.

The sidecar resolves it:

```json
{
  "frameIndex": 6145,
  "timestampMs": 1786646498443,
  "width": 1280,
  "height": 720,
  "bindings": [
    {"slot": 51, "stableId": 51,  "className": "SkeletalMeshComponent", "objectName": "CharacterMesh0",  "serial": 8148, "released": false},
    {"slot": 126,"stableId": 126, "className": "SkeletalMeshComponent", "objectName": "Droid_Head",      "serial": 5423, "released": false},
    {"slot": 10, "stableId": 272, "className": "SplineMeshComponent",   "objectName": "NODE_AddSplineMeshComponent-0", "serial": 0, "released": false}
  ]
}
```

The envelope matters to anyone writing a parser: the top level is an **object**,
not an array, and `bindings` is where the rows live. `frameIndex` is the same
monotonic index as the `.pgm` filename, so a sidecar can be matched to its mask
without parsing the name.

Two per-binding fields carry the identity machinery:

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `serial` | the engine's own serial number for that object. It is half of the `(pointer, serialNumber)` key behind `stableId`, and it is what makes a recycled address detectable rather than silently merging two objects. |
| `released` | the slot's lease had been handed back by the time this frame's table was written. The row is kept rather than dropped, because pixels carrying that id may still be in *this* frame — a released row is how you tell "the label was retired" apart from "the label was never there". |

`stableId` is a 64-bit identity keyed on `(pointer, serialNumber)`. It survives
losing a slot, so an object that goes off screen and comes back resumes its
original track instead of being counted as a new object. Note slot 10 holding
stableId 272 above: slots have been recycled, and the sidecar is what makes that
recoverable rather than corrupting.

The sidecar is written for **every** dumped mask, never separately, and it
describes the table as it stood when that frame's copy was submitted — not when
the mask arrived several frames later. See DEBUGGING.md §7.8 for why that
distinction cost real label accuracy.

## Container

`tools/pack.py` bundles a session into one self-describing `.segcap` file.

```
python tools/pack.py --dir build/bin --out session.segcap --verify
python tools/pack.py --list session.segcap
python tools/pack.py --extract session.segcap --to out/
```

```
magic     8 bytes   "SEGCAP01"
hdrlen    u32
header    utf-8 JSON  {"width":..,"height":..,"codec":..,"records":..,"frames":[..]}
records   ...       each: type u8, frame u64, rawlen u32, complen u32, payload
index     utf-8 JSON  [{type, frame, offset, rawlen, complen}, ...]
idxlen    u32
footer    8 bytes   "SEGCAPIX"
```

The index is at the **end**, with its length in the last 12 bytes. A reader can
seek to any frame without scanning the file, and the writer never has to know
the record layout in advance — the same reason zip puts its directory last.

### Compression lives in the tool, not the DLL

The capture path runs inside a shipped game, on the thread that presents frames.
Everything on it has been kept to the minimum that cannot be done later: a GPU
copy onto the game's own queue, a fence poll, a memcpy out of a mapped readback
buffer. Linking a compressor in there would add third-party code to the game's
address space and CPU time to its present loop, to save disk that is not scarce.

Compression is a pure function of bytes already written. It belongs outside the
process being instrumented.

zlib is the default because it is Python standard library, so a container reads
anywhere with no install step. The codec is recorded **per record**, so adding
zstd later does not invalidate existing files.

### Measured, 75 frames at 1280x720

| | raw | packed | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| masks | 69.1 MB | 0.7 MB | **104.6x** |
| colour frames | 207.4 MB | 115.5 MB | 1.8x |
| sidecars | 1.3 MB | 0.1 MB | 11.9x |
| total | 277.8 MB | 116.3 MB | 2.4x |

Reported separately on purpose. Masks are 8-bit indexed images with large flat
regions — close to the best case for a dictionary coder. Colour frames are
photographic and barely compress. A single "2.4x" would hide both facts and
imply the format does something for colour that it does not.

`--labels-only` omits colour and produces 0.8 MB for the same 75 frames, which
is the useful artifact for anything consuming the labels.

### Two properties enforced in code

**Lossless is verified, not asserted.** `--verify` decompresses every record and
byte-compares it against the file it came from — 225/225 identical on the
session above. A compression bug corrupting one frame in a thousand would
otherwise surface as a mysteriously bad training example months later.

**A mask cannot be packed without its sidecar.** The packer refuses the whole
container if any mask lacks one, because a mask without its slot table is
undecodable rather than merely incomplete. Worth enforcing rather than
documenting and hoping.

```

`docs/INZOI-GENERALIZATION.md`:

```md
# Does any of this generalize? inZOI (UE5, D3D12)

Stray is UE4. Everything measured in this project was measured on one title, and
the renderable allowlist in `customdepth.cpp` literally contains
`ToyoSplineMeshComponent` — Stray's internal prefix. Generalization was the
weakest claim in the project, so it got tested.

**inZOI**: UE5, D3D12-only, 287 MB shipping binary, `BlueClient` project, no
anti-cheat, already installed. It is also a life sim, which turns out to matter.

Every run below is **census mode**: no marking, no GPU work on the game's queue.

---

## Result summary

| layer | generalizes? | evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Injection | **yes** | `VERIFIED: segcap.dll loaded in pid ...` on a 287 MB UE5 binary |
| D3D12 hooking | **yes** | queue sniffed, swapchain hooked, **0 descriptor misses** across 451 targets |
| Render-target election | **yes** | elects a scene-res depth-stencil target and holds it |
| `GUObjectArray` discovery | **yes** | found in 15 ms; 8,719 → 534,153 slots |
| `FName` resolution | **yes** | `block0[0]="None"`, 5 blocks corroborated, names decode correctly |
| Class identification | **yes** | 9,512 distinct classes, 99.8% resolve rate |
| **Property reflection** | **yes, after a fix** | 0 properties → **153** on `UPrimitiveComponent`; see below |
| ProcessEvent discovery | **NO — and it crashed the game** | see below |

Two of the three layers carried over unchanged. The engine layer carried over
further than expected and then stopped at a specific, identifiable place.

---

## What worked, and why

### The D3D12 layer, unchanged

```
captured DIRECT command queue 000001DB4EF83240
backbuffer 2560x1600 format=R10G10B10A2_UNORM
frame 12901: 451 distinct targets observed, 0 descriptor misses
ELECTED 000001DFC482ABC0 (score 200)
```

Nothing in this layer knows what engine it is looking at, and it shows. Queue
sniffing via `ExecuteCommandLists`, descriptor→resource mapping, resource-state
shadowing and the election all worked on first contact.

One detail decided this. inZOI renders its scene at **1280×800 against a
2560×1600 backbuffer** — 50%, presumably DLSS/TSR. The election originally
hard-required backbuffer dimensions and would have rejected every real depth
target, exactly as it did on Stray with `ScreenPercentage=50` (DEBUGGING.md
§7.3). The fix made there — identify the scene cohort by **aspect ratio and
largest of that shape** — is what let this work untouched. A bug fixed properly
on one title generalized; a bug patched with a magic number would not have.

### The object array and FName, unexpectedly

I predicted this would break. UE5 changed a great deal about `FUObjectArray`,
the name pool and the property system, and RESUME.md said so in writing.

```
ue4: FOUND object array at 00007FF64003CBF0 after 15ms
ue4:   NumElements=8719 MaxElements=2162688 NumChunks=1 MaxChunks=33
ue4: FOUND FName blocks, block0[0]="None", 5 further blocks corroborated
ue4: [t+180s] array has 534153 slots
ue4:   resolved=19457  nullObject=1088  failedValidation=0  unreadable=0
```

It found both. The reason is a design choice made months earlier for a different
purpose: the search validates candidates by **structural shape** — chunk counts,
element sizes, pointer plausibility, and whether decoded names are readable text
— rather than matching a version-specific byte pattern. Shape survived the
version change. A signature scan would not have.

Names decode correctly, including inZOI's own classes. Every game prefixes its
types; Stray uses `Toyo`, inZOI uses `B1`:

```
19409  B1Image          17301  HorizontalBoxSlot     8352  Package
 7516  B1HorizontalBox  14574  CanvasPanelSlot       3220  B1Button
 6524  B1TextBlock      10562  ScriptStruct          2143  Texture2D
```

Also worth noting: the first four discovery attempts fail with
`no FChunkedFixedUObjectArray found`, then attempt five succeeds at t≈10s. That
is not a bug, it is the retry loop doing its job — the engine has not built the
array yet at t=2s.

---

## Where it stopped, and how it was fixed

```
introspect: 9512 DISTINCT CLASSES across 246284 objects
introspect: --- PrimitiveComponent : 0 reflected properties ---
introspect: --- SceneComponent : 0 reflected properties ---
```

The classes were found. Walking their property chain returned nothing. This was
the real UE4→UE5 boundary, and everything downstream depended on it: property
reflection is how `bRenderCustomDepth` is located as a packed bit, how
`CustomDepthStencilValue` is written, and how the agent reads the pawn
transform. No properties meant no marking and no perception.

### Step 1: dump the struct instead of guessing

`DumpStructLayout` prints each qword of a `UStruct` and tries to decode it under
both the pre-4.25 and post-4.25 interpretations. Side by side with Stray:

| offset | Stray (UE4) | inZOI (UE5) |
|---|---|---|
| `+0x40` | `SceneComponent` (SuperStruct) | `SceneComponent` — same |
| `+0x48` | `WasRecentlyRendered` (Children) | `WasRecentlyRendered` — same |
| `+0x50` | ptr → decodes `MinDrawDistance` | ptr → decodes **nothing** |

So `ChildProperties` was at the same offset and was a valid pointer. The chain
was there. What had moved was the layout *inside* `FField`.

### Step 2: find the new offset by trying all of them

`ProbeFieldNameOffset` walks every aligned offset in the first 0x48 bytes of the
first field, follows the chain at several candidate `Next` offsets, and prints
which combinations decode into readable names:

```
name@+0x14 next@+0x18 -> 8 links: NavAvoidanceMask, NavAvoidanceMask, NavAvoidanceMask...
name@+0x20 next@+0x18 -> 8 links: MinDrawDistance, LDMaxDrawDistance,
                                  CachedMaxDrawDistance, DepthPriorityGroup
```

The second row is the answer — those are the same four properties, in the same
order, as Stray's UE4 dump. **UE5 shifted `FField` back 8 bytes:
`NamePrivate` 0x28 → 0x20, `Next` 0x20 → 0x18.**

The first row matters too. It decoded eight links, so a test that counted
successful decodes would have accepted it — but every link is the *same name*.
Printing the decoded sample rather than a count is what exposed it, and the
calibration below scores on **distinct** names for that reason.

### Step 3: calibrate at runtime, do not swap one constant for another

`CalibrateFieldLayout()` runs once after discovery on every run. It tries the
candidate offsets against classes known to have properties and keeps whichever
yields the most distinct decoded names. The UE4 values remain the default, so a
build where calibration cannot run behaves exactly as it did before. The same
delta is applied to the `FProperty` fields that follow the header
(`ArrayDim`, `ElementSize`, `OffsetInternal`, and the `FBoolProperty` bit
fields), since the whole struct moved together.

```
ue4: field layout calibrated: name@+0x20 next@+0x18
     (12 distinct names; shift -8 vs UE4.25-4.27)
introspect: --- PrimitiveComponent : 153 reflected properties ---
introspect:   +0x0271  1  BoolProperty  bRenderCustomDepth
introspect:   +0x02A4  4  IntProperty   CustomDepthStencilValue
```

**Both marking properties are found on UE5**, at completely different offsets
from Stray's (`+0x216` mask `0x40`, and `+0x220`) — located by name, which is
the whole point of doing this by reflection.

Verified not to regress UE4: a full Stray capture run after the change produced
201 masks / 200 frames / 201 sidecars, resolved `bRenderCustomDepth` at the
unchanged `+0x216 mask 0x40`, and passed label verification with 0 identities
renamed.

### What is still not done on inZOI

Reflection works, so the route is open, but marking has not been attempted:
`ProcessEvent` discovery still has no UE5 answer, and it is the game-thread
execution point every write depends on. That is the next wall, and unlike this
one it is genuinely dangerous — probing vtable slots is what killed the game
earlier in this session.

---

## Where it stops badly: ProcessEvent, and a crash that was ours

The second census run killed inZOI. The log ends here:

```
ue4: PE candidate 69 -> 1169 valid, 506460 invalid (rejected)
ue4: PE candidate 70 ->  810 valid, 432080 invalid (rejected)
<dead>
```

Finding `ProcessEvent` means hooking UObject vtable slots 60..80 one at a time
and seeing which behaves like it. On Stray that converged on slot 68 with a 4:1
valid ratio. On UE5 the ratios are 1169:506460 and 810:432080 — the probe is
hooking hot functions that are *not* `ProcessEvent` and calling them with
`ProcessEvent`'s signature. One of them took the process down.

**The honest part: this run was described as read-only, and it was not.**

Census mode suppressed GPU work and suppressed UObject writes. It never gated
vtable hooking, because when census mode was written the only mutations worth
thinking about were the ones it did gate. Probing twenty vtable slots on a live
engine is neither a read nor safe, and on an unfamiliar engine it is a loaded
gun.

The mode was doing most of what it promised, which is exactly why nobody noticed
it was not doing all of it. Fixed: census mode now returns before ProcessEvent
discovery and says so in the log.

---

## What this says about the design

Ranked by how well each layer travelled:

1. **Graphics-API-level code generalized completely.** It depends on D3D12, not
   on the engine, and D3D12 does not change between UE versions.
2. **Structural search generalized.** Validating by shape rather than by
   signature was chosen to avoid brittleness against patches; it turned out to
   survive a whole engine major version.
3. **Hardcoded struct offsets did not, and could not.** They are the one place
   the code encodes a specific engine build. That they are confined to a handful
   of named constants in `ue4.cpp` — rather than scattered — is why the fix is
   bounded.

The failure is where a reasonable person would predict, and the parts that
travelled are the parts built to be validated rather than assumed.

---

## inZOI-specific observations

- **It drives itself.** It is a life sim with autonomous agents, so it generates
  evolving gameplay with no input at all. For dataset collection that removes
  the "who plays the game" problem which motivated the closed-loop agent on
  Stray.
- **837 `InstancedStaticMeshComponent`s.** The latent instancing issue flagged
  in the Stray writeup — one component representing many visual instances would
  receive one ID — is live here. Stray never exercised it.
- **The object array is UI-dominated at the menu.** ~90% of the 246k objects at
  the character creator are widgets (`B1Image`, `HorizontalBoxSlot`,
  `CanvasPanelSlot`). Any census taken before reaching a world describes the
  menu, not the game.
- **The screensaver bit again.** `desktop=Screen-saver`, focus impossible, all
  gamepad input discarded — the same failure as DEBUGGING.md §7.1, in a script
  that ported the "disable the setting" half and not the "kill the running one"
  half. It is listed as a known trap in RESUME.md and it still happened.

```

`docs/PIPELINE-STATE.md`:

```md
# What's dynamic, what's baked into a PSO, and why it decided the architecture

The brief's second bullet asks for "understanding what state is dynamic vs baked
into a PSO". That distinction is not a detail here — it is the reason this
project routes per-object IDs through Unreal's CustomDepth pass instead of
writing them itself, and the reason the ID channel is 8 bits wide.

## The split

In D3D12, `ID3D12PipelineState` is immutable and created up front. It bakes:

- shaders, root signature layout, input layout
- blend state, rasterizer state
- **the entire depth-stencil description** — `StencilEnable`, `StencilReadMask`,
  `StencilWriteMask`, and the front/back `StencilFailOp` / `StencilDepthFailOp` /
  `StencilPassOp` / `StencilFunc`
- RTV/DSV formats, sample count

What stays dynamic, set per command list:

- `OMSetRenderTargets` — which targets are bound
- `OMSetStencilRef` — **the stencil reference value**
- `ResourceBarrier`, `ClearDepthStencilView`
- viewports, scissors, blend factor, root arguments, vertex/index buffers

The one piece of stencil behaviour that is *not* baked is the reference value.
Everything that decides whether a write happens at all — enable, write mask,
pass op — is frozen into the PSO at creation.

## Why that killed the obvious approach

The naive plan for per-pixel object IDs is: hook every draw, set a per-object
value, let it land in a stencil or ID buffer.

That cannot work from an injected DLL. To make a draw write an arbitrary ID you
need `StencilEnable = TRUE`, a non-zero `StencilWriteMask`, and
`StencilPassOp = REPLACE`. All three are in the PSO. The game created its PSOs
at load time with its own depth-stencil state, and most of them do not write
stencil at all.

Changing that means **creating new PSOs** — one per distinct combination of
shaders, root signature, input layout, blend and raster state the game uses.
A shipped UE title has thousands. You would have to intercept `SetPipelineState`,
look up or build a stencil-writing twin of whatever PSO was bound, and swap it,
while keeping every other piece of state byte-identical so the frame still
renders correctly. That is not instrumentation any more; it is a shadow renderer,
and every mismatch is a visual artifact in someone's game.

Setting only `OMSetStencilRef` per draw — the one dynamic knob — accomplishes
nothing on its own. The reference value is consumed by the compare and pass
operations, and if the bound PSO has `StencilEnable = FALSE`, it is simply
ignored.

## What we did instead

Let the engine own the PSO problem.

UE's CustomDepth pass already creates PSOs with stencil writes enabled, and
already sets `OMSetStencilRef` per primitive from the primitive's
`CustomDepthStencilValue`. So the intervention needed is not a graphics
intervention at all — it is setting an integer property on a game object and
letting the engine's existing pass do the rendering.

That is why the mutation in this project happens through
`UPrimitiveComponent::SetRenderCustomDepth` on the game thread rather than
anywhere in the D3D12 layer. The renderer hooks stay strictly read-only: no hook
alters an argument, and no hook issues GPU work.

**And it is why the ID is 8 bits.** The width is not a shortcut — it is the width
of the stencil channel of the pass the engine already runs. Getting a wider ID
means owning the PSO, which means the shadow renderer above. The 255-slot
constraint that the identity design works around is structural, imposed by where
the boundary between "instrument" and "rewrite" falls.

## What the census can and cannot see, because of this

We hook eight vtable slots:

| hook | why |
|---|---|
| `Present` | frame boundary, capture point |
| `ExecuteCommandLists` | the command queue is not reachable from the swapchain |
| `CreateRenderTargetView` / `CreateDepthStencilView` | descriptor handle → resource |
| `CreateCommittedResource` | initial resource state, which no barrier announces |
| `ResourceBarrier` | shadow resource state so a copy transition is correct |
| `OMSetRenderTargets` | which targets are bound, and in what order |
| `ClearDepthStencilView` | which targets are cleared each frame |

We deliberately do **not** hook `SetPipelineState`. A consequence worth stating
plainly: the census knows *which* depth target was bound and *how often*, and
that it was cleared — but it does not know what stencil operation the draws
against it were configured to perform, because that lives in the PSO.

This is exactly why the election scores on bind count, clear count, format,
dimensions and persistence rather than on "does this pass write stencil". The
signals it uses are the ones actually observable from dynamic state. An election
that keyed on PSO contents would need a ninth hook and a PSO-desc cache, and
would still not beat "cleared every frame, receives almost no draws" as a
signature for CustomDepth.

## Where it showed up as a bug

The same fact bit during the day-1 RenderDoc analysis. Sampling 12 of 1,365
draws reported "no stencil writes anywhere", which was wrong. Depth-stencil
state is per-PSO, not per-draw, so the correct unit of inspection is the
pipeline object: grouping draws by `pipelineResourceId` and inspecting each
distinct PSO once is **exhaustive** and cheap, where sampling draws is neither.
See `DEBUGGING.md` §2.

## Postscript: the copy path is unaffected

Readback never touches a PSO. `CopyTextureRegion` is not a draw — it needs no
pipeline state, only correct resource states on both sides, which is what the
`ResourceBarrier` shadow provides. That is a large part of why the capture path
could stay read-only with respect to the game's rendering while still doing real
GPU work on its queue.

```

<section>
  <h2>How to read this</h2>
  <p class="lede">
    The brief said the debugging story matters more than the coverage number. So this is
    organised as a build log rather than a summary: it moves forward in time, and where the
    project went wrong it stops and explains the wrong turn in full, including the ones
    where I was confidently wrong for several runs.
  </p>
  <p>Two recurring shapes are worth naming up front, because almost everything below is an
  instance of one of them.</p>
  <div class="callout">
    <span class="tag">Pattern one — roughly two thirds of all time lost</span>
    <p><strong>A measurement that could not observe the thing it was being used to judge,
    reporting the answer that matched my hypothesis.</strong> Not one of these threw an
    exception. Every one produced a plausible number in a log, and I acted on it.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="callout">
    <span class="tag">Pattern two</span>
    <p><strong>Three of my "fixes" made things measurably worse</strong>, because I bounded,
    guarded, or optimised the wrong thing without checking the arithmetic first.</p>
  </div>
  <p>Diagrams in this document are drawn as code rather than generated as images, because
  they encode exact structures — vtable slot numbers, byte offsets, thread boundaries — and
  an approximate picture of a byte offset is worse than no picture.</p>

  <h4>Where it ends up</h4>
  <figure>
    <img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," alt="A Stray gameplay frame with its per-pixel segmentation mask overlaid: the cat, a robot NPC, tree foliage, building faces and steps each rendered in a distinct colour.">
    <figcaption>
      The end state, so the chapters have somewhere to be heading. One captured frame at
      1920×1080: 143 distinct object ids, 98.1% of pixels labelled. The cat is separated
      from the step it stands on; the robot NPC from the tree behind it. The speckle on the
      foliage is real and is discussed in Chapter 10 — UE4 renders dithered LOD as a
      screen-door stipple and CustomDepth inherits it.
    </figcaption>
  </figure>

  <h4>The whole system, and which thread everything runs on</h4>
  <p>Thread ownership is the single most important structural fact here. UObject state
  belongs to the game thread; D3D hooks fire on the render thread; the object-array walk is
  slow and must be on neither.</p>
  <div class="diagram">
    <pre class="mermaid">
flowchart TB
  subgraph RT["RENDER THREAD — read-only w.r.t. the game"]
    PR["Present hook"]
    EL["target election"]
    RB["readback ring<br/>copy + fence poll"]
    WR["write mask + sidecar"]
  end
  subgraph GT["GAME THREAD — via ProcessEvent hook"]
    MK["MarkBatch<br/>WasRecentlyRendered → lease slot →<br/>SetRenderCustomDepth"]
    RV["RefreshVisibility<br/>release slots that left"]
    PC["perception<br/>read pawn transform"]
  end
  subgraph DT["DISCOVERY THREAD"]
    DS["structural search<br/>GUObjectArray + FNamePool"]
    CC["CollectCandidates<br/>full array walk, read-only"]
  end
  subgraph EXT["SEPARATE PROCESS"]
    VP["vpad — ViGEm virtual pad"]
  end
  DS --> MK
  CC --> MK
  MK --> ID["IdentityRegistry<br/>slot lease ↔ stable id"]
  RV --> ID
  ID --> SC["published sidecar<br/>(immutable snapshot)"]
  SC --> WR
  PR --> EL --> RB --> WR
  PC -->|"shared memory<br/>seqlock"| VP
  VP -->|"gamepad input"| GAME(["the game"])
  VP --> AL["action log<br/>(joined by wall clock)"]
    </pre>
  </div>
</section>

<!-- ============================ 0 ============================ -->
<section id="c0">
  <h2>Chapter 0</h2>
  <span class="chapno">Framing and target selection</span>
  <h3>Choosing a game you can be wrong about cheaply</h3>

  <div class="loop">
    <div><div class="k">What</div><div class="v"><p>Pick a target title and a graphics API before writing any code.</p></div></div>
    <div><div class="k">Why</div><div class="v"><p>Every downstream decision depends on it: anti-cheat determines whether injection is possible at all, engine version determines whether reflection works, and iteration speed determines how many wrong turns the week can absorb.</p></div></div>
    <div><div class="k">How</div><div class="v">
      <p>Candidates were assessed on four axes — anti-cheat, engine, iteration cost, and legitimacy of ownership. No pirated builds, on principle and also because repacked executables break vtable hooking.</p>
    </div></div>
    <div><div class="k">Result</div><div class="v"><p><strong>Stray</strong>: UE4, no anti-cheat, no Denuvo, 6 GB, ~40 s to a level, and it accepts <code>-dx12</code>.</p></div></div>
  </div>

  <div class="scroll">
  <table>
    <thead><tr><th>Candidate</th><th>Verdict</th><th>Reason</th></tr></thead>
    <tbody>
      <tr><td>Call of Duty</td><td><span class="chip no">excluded</span></td><td>Ricochet kernel anti-cheat. Injection is both impossible and inappropriate.</td></tr>
      <tr><td>GTA V</td><td><span class="chip no">excluded</span></td><td>Not Unreal, so the entire engine-introspection half of the brief would be unreachable.</td></tr>
      <tr><td>inZOI</td><td><span class="chip part">deferred</span></td><td>UE5, 35 GB, slow iteration. Kept as the generalisation target — which it eventually became.</td></tr>
      <tr><td><strong>Stray</strong></td><td><span class="chip ok">chosen</span></td><td>UE4, D3D12 available, small, fast to load, legitimately owned.</td></tr>
    </tbody>
  </table>
  </div>

  <h4>The D3D11 decision, and being overruled</h4>
  <p>The brief recommends <em>“Unreal with D3D11”</em>. My initial recommendation followed
  it. Part of my stated argument was that going against the recommendation and not
  finishing would read badly.</p>
  <p>That is a status argument, not an engineering one, and it should not have been in the
  analysis. Frank rejected it:</p>
  <blockquote><p>“if d3d12 is hard, let's not running away from it ok? if there's a hardship
  then let's face it”</p></blockquote>
  <p>He was right, and not merely on principle. D3D12 is harder in three specific ways, and
  <em>each one maps onto a bullet in the brief</em>:</p>
  <div class="scroll">
  <table>
    <thead><tr><th>D3D11</th><th>D3D12</th><th>Brief bullet it exercises</th></tr></thead>
    <tbody>
      <tr><td>Device context reachable from the swapchain</td><td>Command queue is <strong>not</strong> reachable from the swapchain by any documented route</td><td>“vtable hooking… Present, OMSetRenderTargets”</td></tr>
      <tr><td>Views are objects with identity</td><td>Descriptor handles are opaque heap offsets carrying no identity</td><td>“render target identification at runtime”</td></tr>
      <tr><td>Runtime tracks resource state</td><td>The application tracks it; an injected DLL must reconstruct it</td><td>“ResourceBarrier”, “copying on the game's own command list”</td></tr>
    </tbody>
  </table>
  </div>
  <p>Choosing D3D11 would have produced a smaller answer to a question that was asking about
  the harder thing.</p>
</section>

<!-- ============================ 1 ============================ -->
<section id="c1">
  <h2>Chapter 1</h2>
  <span class="chapno">Getting code inside the process</span>
  <h3>Three attempts before injection was reliable</h3>

  <div class="loop">
    <div><div class="k">What</div><div class="v"><p>Load <code>segcap.dll</code> into the game process, early enough to hook D3D12 before the game creates its device.</p></div></div>
    <div><div class="k">Why</div><div class="v"><p>Hooks installed after the device exists still work — vtables are shared across instances — but every <em>descriptor view</em> created before we arrive is unrecoverable. A descriptor handle is just a heap offset; without having seen its <code>CreateRTV</code>/<code>CreateDSV</code> call, the resource behind it can never be identified.</p></div></div>
    <div><div class="k">How</div><div class="v"><p><code>CreateRemoteThread</code> + <code>LoadLibraryW</code>, with three modes: <code>--pid</code>, <code>--name</code>, and <code>--launch</code> (create suspended, inject, resume).</p></div></div>
    <div><div class="k">Result</div><div class="v"><p>Eventually <strong>0 descriptor misses</strong> — but only after defeating Steam, which took the rest of this chapter.</p></div></div>
  </div>

  <div class="fail">
    <p class="hdr">Failure</p>
    <h5>RenderDoc reported success while nothing was hooked</h5>
    <dl>
      <dt>Symptom</dt><dd><p><code>renderdoccmd</code> printed <code>Launched as ID 38920</code>. No capture appeared and F12 did nothing.</p></dd>
      <dt>Cause</dt><dd>
        <p><code>renderdoc.dll</code> was absent from both Stray processes. The parent chain explains it:</p>
        <pre class="log">steam.exe → Stray.exe (shim) → Stray-Win64-Shipping.exe</pre>
        <p>The launcher we hooked is a shim; the renderer is its child.</p>
      </dd>
      <dt>Fix</dt><dd><p><code>--opt-hook-children</code> plus a <code>%command%</code> wrapper. Later replaced entirely by <code>--watch</code>, which polls for the process by name and injects the instant it appears.</p></dd>
      <dt>Lesson</dt><dd><p>“Launched successfully” describes the launcher, not the hook. The injector now <em>verifies module presence</em> in the target rather than reporting its own success.</p></dd>
    </dl>
  </div>

  <div class="fail">
    <p class="hdr">Failure</p>
    <h5>Suspended launch was useless on its own — 950 missed descriptors</h5>
    <dl>
      <dt>Symptom</dt><dd><p><code>--launch</code> created the process suspended, injected, and resumed. The game ran. We still missed ~950 descriptors.</p></dd>
      <dt>Cause</dt><dd><p><code>LoadLibraryW</code> returns as soon as <code>DllMain</code> returns, and <code>DllMain</code> only spawns a worker thread — it must, because creating a D3D12 device under the loader lock can deadlock the host. So the injector resumed the game while we were still building dummy devices to read vtables from. Measured window: ~300 ms.</p></dd>
      <dt>Fix</dt><dd><p>A named-event handshake. The injector creates <code>Local\segcap_hooks_ready_&lt;pid&gt;</code> before injecting and waits on it; the DLL signals once all hooks are installed. Misses went <strong>950 → 0</strong>.</p></dd>
    </dl>
  </div>

  <div class="fail">
    <p class="hdr">Failure — and the fix that unlocked the whole harness</p>
    <h5><code>SteamAPI_RestartAppIfNecessary</code> made suspended launch impossible</h5>
    <dl>
      <dt>Symptom</dt><dd><p>Launching the shipping executable directly: it starts, exits within a second, and Steam launches a fresh copy. The process we injected into was never the one that rendered.</p></dd>
      <dt>Cause</dt><dd><p>Steamworks games call <code>SteamAPI_RestartAppIfNecessary</code> at startup. Launched outside Steam, it asks Steam to relaunch and exits.</p></dd>
      <dt>Fix</dt><dd><p>Write <code>steam_appid.txt</code> containing the app id next to the executable. This is the documented Steamworks mechanism telling the API “this process <em>is</em> the app”, and it makes the call a no-op. Steam still has to be running — it is not a DRM bypass, it is what Steamworks ships for developers running their own builds.</p></dd>
      <dt>Payoff</dt><dd>
        <p>One 8-byte file unlocked three things at once:</p>
        <ul>
          <li>injection before the first D3D call → <strong>0 descriptor misses</strong></li>
          <li><code>-windowed</code>, removing the fullscreen mode switch that broke focus for four consecutive runs (Chapter 9)</li>
          <li><code>-ResX/-ResY</code>, cutting readback bandwidth to a quarter while debugging</li>
        </ul>
      </dd>
    </dl>
  </div>
</section>

<!-- ============================ 2 ============================ -->
<section id="c2">
  <h2>Chapter 2</h2>
  <span class="chapno">Reconnaissance</span>
  <h3>Ask the frame what it contains before writing a capture system</h3>

  <div class="loop">
    <div><div class="k">What</div><div class="v"><p>Capture one Stray frame in RenderDoc and answer: does a CustomDepth target exist, and does anything write stencil into it?</p></div></div>
    <div><div class="k">Why</div><div class="v"><p>If UE's CustomDepth pass is disabled in this build, the entire planned route is dead and it is better to know on day one than day five.</p></div></div>
    <div><div class="k">How</div><div class="v"><p>RenderDoc's Python API, driven headless over a saved <code>.rdc</code>.</p></div></div>
    <div><div class="k">Result</div><div class="v"><p>Three full-res <code>D32S8</code> targets. Two receive draws; <strong><code>ResourceId::1932</code> is cleared every frame and receives none</strong> — the signature of CustomDepth with no opt-ins.</p></div></div>
  </div>

  <div class="fail">
    <p class="hdr">Failure — the most instructive of the project</p>
    <h5>Defensive <code>getattr</code> turned wrong field names into confident zeros</h5>
    <dl>
      <dt>Symptom</dt><dd>
        <p>The first analysis reported four facts. All four were wrong:</p>
        <pre class="log">backbuffer            8160x8160
full-res stencil      0
depth-stencil clears  0
debug names present   12592/12592</pre>
      </dd>
      <dt>Cause</dt><dd><p>The script was written against <em>assumed</em> RenderDoc API field names, wrapped in <code>getattr</code> chains with <code>None</code> fallbacks. A wrong guess returned <code>None</code>, which the caller rendered as zero. The resolution came from a heuristic — “largest colour texture” — which picked a shadow atlas.</p></dd>
      <dt>Fix</dt><dd><p><code>rdc_probe_api.py</code>: dump the real attributes of every object <em>before</em> using it, then write the analysis against facts. Read failures now report rather than degrade.</p></dd>
      <dt>Lesson</dt><dd><p>When probing an unfamiliar API, defensive fallbacks are actively harmful. They convert <em>“I don't know this API”</em> into <em>“here is your answer.”</em> A crash would have been more useful than any of those four numbers.</p></dd>
    </dl>
  </div>

  <div class="fail">
    <p class="hdr">Failure</p>
    <h5>Sampling 12 of 1,365 draws and reporting absence</h5>
    <dl>
      <dt>Symptom</dt><dd><p><code>writes stencil: no</code> for Stray's scene depth.</p></dd>
      <dt>Cause</dt><dd><p>The scan sampled every ~113th draw. UE's CustomDepth pass is a handful of draws; that sampling misses it nearly every time. The result meant “I did not look hard enough”, not “there is no stencil”.</p></dd>
      <dt>Fix</dt><dd><p>Depth-stencil state is <strong>baked into the PSO</strong>, so grouping draws by <code>pipelineResourceId</code> and inspecting each distinct pipeline object <em>once</em> is exhaustive <em>and</em> cheaper than sampling. Taken directly from the brief's own “dynamic vs baked into a PSO”.</p></dd>
    </dl>
  </div>

  <div class="fail">
    <p class="hdr">Failure</p>
    <h5><code>SetFrameEvent(force=True)</code> ran for twenty minutes</h5>
    <dl>
      <dt>Symptom</dt><dd><p>The analysis appeared to hang.</p></dd>
      <dt>Cause</dt><dd><p><code>force=True</code> replays the frame from the start for every event. Across 1,365 draws that is quadratic.</p></dd>
      <dt>Fix</dt><dd><p><code>force=False</code>, and <code>GetUsage()</code> for per-resource read/write facts, which needs no replay at all. Runtime went to seconds.</p></dd>
    </dl>
  </div>
</section>

<!-- ============================ 3 ============================ -->
<section id="c3">
  <h2>Chapter 3</h2>
  <span class="chapno">Intercepting D3D12</span>
  <h3>Reconstructing the bookkeeping D3D11 used to do for you</h3>

  <p>D3D12 moved bookkeeping from the runtime into the application. For an injected DLL,
  “the application” is the game — so that bookkeeping becomes ours to reconstruct from the
  outside. Three things have to be recovered before a single pixel can be copied.</p>

  <div class="diagram">
    <pre class="mermaid">
flowchart LR
  subgraph GAME["Stray process"]
    direction TB
    SC["IDXGISwapChain3"]
    DEV["ID3D12Device"]
    Q["ID3D12CommandQueue"]
    CL["ID3D12GraphicsCommandList"]
  end
  subgraph HOOKS["segcap hooks (read-only)"]
    direction TB
    H1["Present (8)"]
    H2["ExecuteCommandLists (10)"]
    H3["CreateRTV (20)<br/>CreateDSV (21)"]
    H4["CreateCommittedResource (27)"]
    H5["ResourceBarrier (26)"]
    H6["OMSetRenderTargets (46)"]
    H7["ClearDepthStencilView (47)"]
  end
  SC --> H1
  Q --> H2
  DEV --> H3
  DEV --> H4
  CL --> H5
  CL --> H6
  CL --> H7
  H2 -->|"queue pointer"| ST["captured queue"]
  H3 -->|"handle → resource"| MAP["descriptor map"]
  H4 -->|"initial state"| SHADOW["state shadow"]
  H5 -->|"StateAfter"| SHADOW
  H6 -->|"which target, how often"| CENSUS["target census"]
  H7 -->|"cleared this frame"| CENSUS
    </pre>
  </div>

  <h4>Problem 1 — the command queue is not reachable from the swapchain</h4>
  <div class="loop">
    <div><div class="k">Why it matters</div><div class="v"><p>Any GPU work we submit must go on a queue. There is no documented route from <code>IDXGISwapChain</code> to the <code>ID3D12CommandQueue</code> it presents on.</p></div></div>
    <div><div class="k">How</div><div class="v"><p>Hook <code>ID3D12CommandQueue::ExecuteCommandLists</code> (slot 10) and capture the <code>this</code> pointer of the first <code>DIRECT</code>-type queue that submits work. The device is then resolved from the queue via <code>GetDevice</code>.</p></div></div>
    <div><div class="k">Result</div><div class="v"><pre class="log">captured DIRECT command queue 00000151D3496D80
resolved device 00000151D349A160 from queue</pre></div></div>
  </div>

  <h4>Problem 2 — descriptor handles carry no identity</h4>
  <div class="loop">
    <div><div class="k">Why it matters</div><div class="v"><p><code>OMSetRenderTargets</code> receives <code>D3D12_CPU_DESCRIPTOR_HANDLE</code> values, which are heap offsets. Nothing in them says which resource is bound.</p></div></div>
    <div><div class="k">How</div><div class="v"><p><code>CreateRenderTargetView</code> and <code>CreateDepthStencilView</code> see <em>both</em> the resource and the destination handle. Recording <code>handle.ptr → ID3D12Resource*</code> at creation is what makes the handles meaningful later. This is the whole reason early injection matters.</p></div></div>
    <div><div class="k">Result</div><div class="v"><p><strong>0 descriptor misses</strong> across 451 distinct targets, on both games tested.</p></div></div>
  </div>

  <h4>Problem 3 — resource state must be shadowed</h4>
  <div class="loop">
    <div><div class="k">Why it matters</div><div class="v"><p>Copying a depth target requires transitioning it to <code>COPY_SOURCE</code> and back. That transition needs the correct <code>StateBefore</code>. A wrong guess is a debug-layer error at best and a GPU hang at worst.</p></div></div>
    <div><div class="k">How</div><div class="v"><p><code>ResourceBarrier</code> is hooked and every <code>Transition.StateAfter</code> recorded. <em>And</em> — a subtlety that only showed up on the fixture — resources carry an <strong>initial state that no barrier ever announces</strong>. A depth buffer created in <code>DEPTH_WRITE</code> and never transitioned reads back as <code>COMMON</code> from a barrier-only shadow. So <code>CreateCommittedResource</code> is hooked too, purely to seed the map.</p></div></div>
    <div><div class="k">Result</div><div class="v"><p>Correct transitions on both titles, no debug-layer errors, no hangs attributable to state.</p></div></div>
  </div>

  <h4>The insight that decided the architecture</h4>
  <div class="callout">
    <span class="tag">Dynamic vs PSO-baked</span>
    <p>In D3D12, <code>StencilEnable</code>, <code>StencilWriteMask</code> and the pass/fail
    operations are all <strong>baked into the pipeline state object</strong>. The only
    dynamic piece is the reference value.</p>
  </div>
  <p>So the obvious plan — hook every draw, set a per-object value, let it land in stencil —
  <em>cannot work from an injected DLL</em>. To make the game's draws write arbitrary IDs
  you need <code>StencilEnable = TRUE</code>, a non-zero write mask and
  <code>StencilPassOp = REPLACE</code>, all frozen at PSO creation. Changing that means
  intercepting <code>SetPipelineState</code> and swapping in a stencil-writing twin of
  whatever was bound — one per distinct combination of shaders, root signature, input
  layout, blend and raster state. A shipped UE title has thousands. That is a shadow
  renderer, not instrumentation, and every mismatch is a visual artifact in someone's game.</p>
  <p>Setting <code>OMSetStencilRef</code> alone accomplishes nothing: if the bound PSO has
  <code>StencilEnable = FALSE</code>, the reference value is simply ignored.</p>
  <p><strong>Hence routing through UE's CustomDepth pass</strong>, which already has
  stencil-writing PSOs and already feeds <code>CustomDepthStencilValue</code> to
  <code>OMSetStencilRef</code> per primitive. The intervention becomes setting an integer on
  a game object. The D3D12 hooks stay strictly read-only — none alters an argument, none
  issues GPU work.</p>
  <p><strong>And it is why the ID is 8 bits.</strong> Not a shortcut: it is the width of the
  pass the engine already runs. The 255-slot constraint that Chapter 8 works around is
  structural, imposed by where the line between instrumenting and rewriting falls.</p>
  <p>One honest consequence: <code>SetPipelineState</code> is deliberately <em>not</em>
  hooked, so the census knows which depth target was bound and how often, but not what
  stencil operation its draws were configured to perform. That is exactly why the election
  in the next chapter scores on bind count, clear count, format and persistence — the
  signals actually observable from dynamic state.</p>
</section>

<!-- ============================ 4 ============================ -->
<section id="c4">
  <h2>Chapter 4</h2>
  <span class="chapno">Electing the right buffer</span>
  <h3>Finding one resource among 451, with no names</h3>

  <div class="loop">
    <div><div class="k">What</div><div class="v"><p>Identify, at runtime, which of the game's depth-stencil targets is the CustomDepth buffer.</p></div></div>
    <div><div class="k">Why</div><div class="v"><p>Debug names are stripped in shipping builds. The brief is explicit: elect by format, dimensions, resource state and bind order. An election that leans on debug names is a technique that only works where it is not needed.</p></div></div>
    <div><div class="k">How</div><div class="v">
      <p>Score every observed target each frame:</p>
      <ul>
        <li><strong>Hard rejects</strong> — no stencil plane; not at scene resolution; is the most-bound target in the frame (that is scene depth).</li>
        <li><strong>Positive</strong> — single-sample; cleared every frame; few or no draws; persistent across the session.</li>
        <li><strong>Tie-break</strong> — by resource address, deterministically.</li>
      </ul>
    </div></div>
    <div><div class="k">Result</div><div class="v"><p>Stable election on both games. It took three rounds and one fix that made things worse.</p></div></div>
  </div>

  <div class="diagram">
    <pre class="mermaid">
flowchart TD
  A["target observed<br/>this session"] --> B{"has stencil<br/>plane?"}
  B -- no --> R1["reject"]
  B -- yes --> C{"at scene<br/>resolution?"}
  C -- no --> R2["reject: shadow map<br/>or downsample"]
  C -- yes --> D{"most-bound<br/>target?"}
  D -- yes --> R3["reject: scene depth<br/>(engine owns its stencil)"]
  D -- no --> E["base score 100"]
  E --> F["+20 single sample"]
  F --> G["+cleared every frame"]
  G --> H["+persistent across session"]
  H --> I{"incumbent AND<br/>has produced a<br/>non-empty mask?"}
  I -- yes --> J["+40 earned incumbency"]
  I -- no --> K["no bonus"]
  J --> L["rank, tie-break by address"]
  K --> L
    </pre>
  </div>

  <h4>Round 1 — 1,085 election changes in one session</h4>
  <div class="fail">
    <p class="hdr">Failure</p>
    <h5>A tie broken by <code>std::sort</code> is a coin flip re-tossed 30 times a second</h5>
    <dl>
      <dt>Symptom</dt><dd>
        <pre class="log">version                          frames  census blocks  ≈changes
per-frame signals only             4201           1099     ~1085</pre>
        <p>Elections split 541 / 540 between two candidates.</p>
      </dd>
      <dt>Cause</dt><dd><p>Two candidates scored <strong>identically</strong> at +200, and ties fell to <code>std::sort</code>'s ordering of equal elements. Worse, both winners were <em>transient loading-screen depth buffers</em> alive for 25 seconds; the real candidate lived all 118.</p></dd>
      <dt>Fix</dt><dd><p>Deterministic tie-break by resource address, plus a persistence signal so a buffer that has existed for the whole session outranks one that appeared during a load.</p></dd>
    </dl>
  </div>

  <h4>Round 2 — a fix that made things worse</h4>
  <div class="fail">
    <p class="hdr">Fix that made things worse</p>
    <h5>Persistence scoring left scene depth <em>electable</em></h5>
    <dl>
      <dt>Change</dt><dd><p>Added a +60 persistence bonus.</p></dd>
      <dt>Result</dt><dd><p>Scene depth — whose stencil bits UE4 fully owns for lighting channels, decals and the sandbox flag — went from <code>-200</code> to <strong><code>+10</code></strong>. Still positive. Still electable.</p></dd>
      <dt>Why that is severe</dt><dd><p>Electing scene depth would have produced masks made of <em>lighting-channel bits</em> that look like a plausible segmentation and mean nothing. A confidently wrong mask is worse than no mask.</p></dd>
      <dt>Fix</dt><dd><p>Scene depth became a <strong>hard rejection</strong>, not a penalty. “No viable candidate this frame” is the correct answer in that situation.</p></dd>
    </dl>
  </div>

  <h4>Round 3 — the ballot itself was wrong</h4>
  <div class="fail">
    <p class="hdr">Failure</p>
    <h5>A candidate absent from a frame was absent from the ballot</h5>
    <dl>
      <dt>Symptom</dt><dd><p>Still flapping after persistence, incumbency and deterministic tie-break.</p></dd>
      <dt>Cause</dt><dd><p><code>targets_</code> was rebuilt from scratch every frame. A candidate not bound <em>or</em> cleared in a given frame was not on the ballot at all — and an incumbency bonus cannot help something that is not standing. Two candidates alternating their absence traded the win back and forth.</p></dd>
      <dt>Fix</dt><dd><p>Elect from <strong>accumulated evidence</strong> across the session, with entries pruned after 600 unseen frames so a destroyed buffer cannot win on stale persistence.</p></dd>
      <dt>Result</dt><dd>
        <pre class="log">version                                        frames  blocks  ≈changes
per-frame signals only                           4201    1099     ~1085
+ persistence, incumbency, deterministic tie     5101     141      ~124
+ accumulated evidence                           2701      11        ~2</pre>
      </dd>
    </dl>
  </div>

  <h4>Round 4 — the rule that was never sound</h4>
  <div class="fail">
    <p class="hdr">Failure</p>
    <h5>The census reported that a 3D game had no depth buffer</h5>
    <dl>
      <dt>Symptom</dt><dd><p>In-level, the census contained exactly one depth-stencil target: a 1×1 dummy. Read literally: a 3D game rendering without depth. The log stated it flatly and nothing errored.</p></dd>
      <dt>Diagnosis</dt><dd>
        <p>The census can only report targets it successfully <em>resolved</em>, so it cannot distinguish “absent” from “filtered out by me”. Logging every distinct resource passed to <code>CreateDepthStencilView</code>, upstream of the filter, answered it in one run:</p>
        <pre class="log">CreateDSV #2: R32G8X24_TYPELESS 640x360 ... D32_FLOAT_S8X24_UINT
CreateDSV #5: R32G8X24_TYPELESS 640x360
CreateDSV #6: R32G8X24_TYPELESS 640x360</pre>
      </dd>
      <dt>Cause</dt><dd><p>640×360 against a 1280×720 backbuffer — the game was running <code>ScreenPercentage=50</code>. The election hard-required dimensions <em>equal to the backbuffer</em>.</p></dd>
      <dt>Fix</dt><dd><p>That rule was never sound: screen percentage, dynamic resolution and upsampling are all normal. Replaced with <em>“matches the backbuffer's aspect ratio, and is the largest of that shape”</em> — square shadow atlases and fractional downsample chains fall out automatically.</p></dd>
      <dt>Payoff</dt><dd><p>This fix later let the entire election work <strong>unchanged</strong> on inZOI, which renders 1280×800 into a 2560×1600 backbuffer. A bug fixed properly generalised; a magic number would not have.</p></dd>
    </dl>
  </div>

  <h4>Round 5 — incumbency cemented a first-frame guess</h4>
  <div class="fail">
    <p class="hdr">Failure</p>
    <h5>+40 for being elected, granted before there was anything to protect</h5>
    <dl>
      <dt>Symptom</dt><dd>
        <pre class="log">+270  CFB02B30  few binds (2) => CustomDepth pass; INCUMBENT   ← 230 + 40
+250  EEA5320   cleared but never bound => CustomDepth with no opt-ins</pre>
        <p>Every mask came back empty for an entire session.</p>
      </dd>
      <dt>Cause</dt><dd><p>The first election ran at <strong>frame 2</strong>, when only one scene-res candidate had been observed at all. It scored 200 and became incumbent. Two frames later the real CustomDepth target appeared and scored 250 on its own merits — but 230+40 beat it every frame thereafter.</p></dd>
      <dt>Fix</dt><dd><p>Incumbency must be <strong>earned, not granted</strong>. The bonus now applies only once the elected target has produced a non-empty mask. A target that has never yielded a single non-zero pixel has no stream worth protecting, so the election stays free to correct itself.</p></dd>
    </dl>
  </div>
</section>

<!-- ============================ 5 ============================ -->
<section id="c5">
  <h2>Chapter 5</h2>
  <span class="chapno">Readback</span>
  <h3>Getting the stencil plane to the CPU without stalling the render thread</h3>

  <div class="loop">
    <div><div class="k">What</div><div class="v"><p>Copy the stencil plane of the elected target into CPU-visible memory, once per frame, without ever blocking.</p></div></div>
    <div><div class="k">Why</div><div class="v"><p>A blocking readback serialises CPU and GPU and would be visible to the player as a frame-rate collapse. The brief asks for “fences and an async ring so you never stall the render thread”.</p></div></div>
    <div><div class="k">How</div><div class="v">
      <ul>
        <li><code>CopyTextureRegion</code> with <code>PlaneSlice = 1</code> — the stencil plane of a depth-stencil resource is a separate sub-resource plane, and there is no D3D11 equivalent of addressing it directly.</li>
        <li>Destination in a <code>D3D12_HEAP_TYPE_READBACK</code> buffer, laid out with <code>D3D12_TEXTURE_DATA_PITCH_ALIGNMENT</code> (256-byte rows).</li>
        <li>A <strong>3-deep ring</strong> of (allocator, command list, readback buffer, fence value).</li>
        <li>Collection polls <code>GetCompletedValue</code> — <strong>never</strong> <code>SetEventOnCompletion</code> + <code>Wait</code>.</li>
      </ul>
    </div></div>
    <div><div class="k">Result</div><div class="v"><p>Sustained ~60 submissions/second with <code>dropped=0</code>, verified against a ground-truth fixture before ever touching the game.</p></div></div>
  </div>

  <div class="diagram">
    <pre class="mermaid">
sequenceDiagram
  participant P as Present hook
  participant R as readback ring (3 slots)
  participant Q as game command queue
  participant D as Drain
  P->>R: Prepare(layout) — no-op if unchanged
  P->>R: Enqueue(frame N)
  R->>R: barrier target → COPY_SOURCE
  R->>R: CopyTextureRegion PlaneSlice=1
  R->>R: barrier back to shadowed state
  R->>Q: ExecuteCommandLists + Signal(fence, N)
  Note over P,Q: no wait here — the render thread returns
  P->>D: Drain() next frame
  D->>R: GetCompletedValue() ≥ slot fence?
  R-->>D: yes → map, memcpy, unmap, recycle slot
    </pre>
  </div>

  <div class="fail">
    <p class="hdr">Crash — the only one caused by our code in Stray</p>
    <h5><code>Prepare</code> keyed on the resource pointer, and swapchains rotate</h5>
    <dl>
      <dt>Symptom</dt><dd><p>Stray exited mid-run: <code>game exited early -- possible crash</code>. Appeared immediately after adding colour-frame capture.</p></dd>
      <dt>Cause</dt><dd>
        <p>A swapchain rotates between several backbuffers, so <code>GetBuffer(GetCurrentBackBufferIndex())</code> returns a <em>different</em> <code>ID3D12Resource*</code> each frame. <code>Prepare</code> compared the resource <strong>pointer</strong> to decide whether it was already initialised:</p>
        <pre class="log">if (preparedFor_ == target &amp;&amp; width_ == desc.Width &amp;&amp; ...) return true;</pre>
        <p>So every frame it believed it had a new target, called <code>ReleaseResources()</code> — destroying readback buffers and command lists <strong>while copies were still in flight</strong> — and rebuilt them. A resource-destruction storm on the render thread.</p>
      </dd>
      <dt>Fix</dt><dd><p>Key on the <strong>layout</strong> — width, height, format, plane slice — not the pointer. Only layout determines ring sizing, and <code>Enqueue</code> already receives the actual resource to copy from, so a rotating source needs no special handling at all.</p></dd>
      <dt>What I should have done</dt><dd><p>Verified on the fixture first. The <code>d3d12_testapp</code> fixture has a 3-buffer swapchain and reproduces the exact rotation; it caught the fix in <strong>12 seconds</strong> without touching the user's game. I went straight to Stray because the feature “obviously” only mattered there.</p></dd>
    </dl>
  </div>

  <h5>The fixture, and why it existed before any of this</h5>
  <p><code>d3d12_testapp</code> renders a 4×4 grid of quads writing known stencil values
  1–16 at known pixel coordinates. Every piece of the capture layer was developed against it
  first. Its validator asserts each quad carries its expected ID at its expected pixel —
  16 regions, 28,224 pixels each, exact centroids. That is ground truth in the strict
  sense: the correct answer is known independently of the thing being tested.</p>
</section>

<!-- ============================ 6 ============================ -->
<section id="c6">
  <h2>Chapter 6</h2>
  <span class="chapno">Reading the engine</span>
  <h3>Finding UE's object graph in a stripped 84 MB binary</h3>

  <div class="loop">
    <div><div class="k">What</div><div class="v"><p>Locate <code>GUObjectArray</code> and the <code>FName</code> pool, then read any object's class, name and properties.</p></div></div>
    <div><div class="k">Why</div><div class="v"><p>Every remaining step needs it. Marking needs <code>bRenderCustomDepth</code>; the sidecar needs class and object names; the agent needs the pawn transform. Without reflection there is no mask that means anything.</p></div></div>
    <div><div class="k">How</div><div class="v">
      <p><strong>Structural search, not byte patterns.</strong> Scan <code>.data</code> for a candidate <code>FChunkedFixedUObjectArray</code> and validate by <em>shape</em>: chunk count consistent with element count, 65,536 elements per chunk, chunk pointers readable, and the first few entries decoding as objects whose class pointers themselves decode as classes.</p>
      <p>Byte-pattern scanning was rejected deliberately — it breaks on every patch, and on a different engine version. Shape does not.</p>
    </div></div>
    <div><div class="k">Result</div><div class="v">
      <pre class="log">ue4: FOUND object array at 00007FF6D0D84FD0 after 15ms
ue4:   NumElements=173598 MaxElements=2162688 NumChunks=3
ue4: FOUND FName blocks, block0[0]="None", 5 blocks corroborated</pre>
      <p>Proof it is correct: resolved names came back as UE4's class hierarchy <em>in registration order</em> — <code>Object → Actor → ActorComponent → SceneComponent → PrimitiveComponent → MeshComponent → SkinnedMeshComponent</code>. That cannot happen by chance.</p>
    </div></div>
  </div>

  <h4><code>IsReadable</code>, and the six bugs one stale snapshot caused</h4>
  <p>Walking a live process's memory looking for a structure by shape means touching bad
  addresses is <em>expected</em>, not exceptional. <code>IsReadable</code> answers “can I
  dereference this?” from a cached map of committed regions, binary-searched — a linear
  walk over a few thousand regions across millions of checks turns the scan into an
  apparent hang.</p>

  <div class="fail">
    <p class="hdr">Failure — one root cause, six distinct symptoms</p>
    <h5>The map is a snapshot; the game allocates constantly</h5>
    <dl>
      <dt>The shape</dt><dd><p>When the map went stale, <code>IsReadable</code> rejected valid addresses and every caller interpreted <em>“I can't see this”</em> as <em>“this isn't what I'm looking for.”</em> <strong>Failing closed looks like a finding.</strong></p></dd>
      <dt>Symptoms</dt><dd>
        <div class="scroll">
        <table>
          <thead><tr><th>#</th><th>What the log said</th><th>Reality</th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr><td class="num">1</td><td>resolved object count <em>dropped</em> as the level loaded</td><td>new chunks invisible</td></tr>
            <tr><td class="num">2</td><td><code>PrimitiveComponent descendants: 622</code></td><td>actually 38,479</td></tr>
            <tr><td class="num">3</td><td><code>unreadable=8165</code> of a 21,273 sample</td><td>array grew 196k → 319k slots</td></tr>
            <tr><td class="num">4</td><td>PE candidate 68: <code>30145 valid / 0 invalid</code>, then <code>742 / 654</code></td><td><code>UFunction</code>s in new memory counted as “not a UFunction”</td></tr>
            <tr><td class="num">5</td><td>only 267 of ~29,000 primitives marked</td><td>walk never refreshed</td></tr>
            <tr><td class="num">6</td><td><code>ProcessEvent not found in slots 60..80</code></td><td>same as #4 — sank the entire run</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
        </div>
      </dd>
      <dt>Fix</dt><dd><p>Refresh before every walk, and before every ProcessEvent candidate.</p></dd>
      <dt>Later</dt><dd><p>This same map caused the project's second crash, months later — see Chapter 9.</p></dd>
    </dl>
  </div>

  <div class="fail">
    <p class="hdr">Failure</p>
    <h5>Name lookup returned a structurally valid, completely empty class</h5>
    <dl>
      <dt>Symptom</dt><dd><p><code>0 properties declared directly on UPrimitiveComponent</code>, all four required properties <code>MISSING</code>. Two runs spent suspecting my <code>FField</code> and <code>UStruct</code> offsets.</p></dd>
      <dt>Cause</dt><dd><p>My offsets were <strong>correct the entire time</strong>. <code>FindClass</code> matched the first object named <code>PrimitiveComponent</code> whose class was <code>Class</code> — and that object had <code>Children</code> <em>and</em> <code>ChildProperties</code> both null. Structurally coherent (its <code>NumStructBasesInChainMinusOne</code> was 3, the correct inheritance depth) but unpopulated.</p></dd>
      <dt>Diagnosis</dt><dd><p>Get the same class a <strong>second independent way</strong> — read <code>ClassPrivate</code> off a live <code>StaticMeshComponent</code> instance — and compare. Different pointer, fully populated, <code>ChildProperties</code> at <code>+0x50</code> decoding to <code>"ForcedLodModel"</code>.</p></dd>
      <dt>Fix</dt><dd><p><code>FindClass</code> now requires a non-null property chain and reports how many stubs it skipped.</p></dd>
      <dt>Lesson</dt><dd><p>When a lookup returns something that <em>looks</em> right but is empty, the fastest disambiguation is a second, independent route to the same object.</p></dd>
    </dl>
  </div>

  <div class="fail">
    <p class="hdr">Failure — silent, and the most dangerous in the project</p>
    <h5><code>bRenderCustomDepth</code> is a packed bit, not a byte</h5>
    <dl>
      <dt>Symptom</dt><dd><p><strong>None.</strong> Reflection reported it at <code>+0x216</code>, size 1. Everything looked fine.</p></dd>
      <dt>Cause</dt><dd>
        <p>Seven properties printed at the <em>same offset</em> <code>+0x212</code>:</p>
        <pre class="log">+0x212  size=1  bReceivesDecals
+0x212  size=1  bOwnerNoSee
+0x212  size=1  bRenderInMainPass
+0x212  size=1  bUseAsOccluder
...</pre>
        <p>UE packs bools into individual bits of a shared byte. Writing <code>1</code> to the whole byte would have silently flipped <code>bUseAsOccluder</code>, <code>bSelectable</code> and the occlusion/visibility flags — <em>precisely</em> the “did you change what the player sees” failure the brief asks about, and it would have looked like it worked.</p>
      </dd>
      <dt>Fix</dt><dd><p>Read <code>FBoolProperty::FieldMask</code> at <code>+0x7B</code>. Every write is read-modify-write, then verified by reading back and asserting <strong>only</strong> the masked bit changed. If anything else moved, the original byte is restored and the write is counted as rejected.</p></dd>
      <dt>Honest note</dt><dd><p>This surfaced only because seven names printed at one offset — visible only because I had made the probe verbose two steps earlier for an unrelated reason. A lucky catch, not foresight.</p></dd>
    </dl>
  </div>

  <h4>ProcessEvent — a safe execution point on the game thread</h4>
  <div class="loop">
    <div><div class="k">What</div><div class="v"><p>Find <code>UObject::ProcessEvent</code> so engine functions can be invoked on the thread that owns UObject state.</p></div></div>
    <div><div class="k">Why</div><div class="v"><p>Our D3D hooks run on the render thread. Mutating UObject state from there is a data race that can work a thousand times and then corrupt something. And Chapter 7 shows a raw property write is not sufficient anyway.</p></div></div>
    <div><div class="k">How</div><div class="v"><p>No signature scan. Hook UObject vtable slots 60–80 one at a time and <strong>validate by behaviour</strong>: for each call, check whether argument 2 is a pointer to something that passes a <code>UFunction</code> test. The real ProcessEvent shows a decisive ratio.</p></div></div>
    <div><div class="k">Result</div><div class="v">
      <pre class="log">ue4: ProcessEvent CONFIRMED at vtable index 68
ue4: &gt;&gt;&gt; task executed on game thread 26900 &lt;&lt;&lt;</pre>
      <p>Proven, not assumed — the confirmation is a task actually running on the game thread and reporting its own thread id.</p>
    </div></div>
  </div>
  <p>This probe is also the most dangerous code in the project: it hooks arbitrary vtable
  slots on a live engine and calls them with ProcessEvent's signature. On UE4 it converges.
  On UE5 it killed the game — Chapter 12.</p>
</section>

<!-- ============================ 7 ============================ -->
<section id="c7">
  <h2>Chapter 7</h2>
  <span class="chapno">Making the buffer contain something</span>
  <h3>Three runs concluding “CustomDepth doesn't work”</h3>

  <div class="loop">
    <div><div class="k">What</div><div class="v"><p>Set <code>bRenderCustomDepth = true</code> and a per-object <code>CustomDepthStencilValue</code> on visible primitives, so the CustomDepth pass has something to draw.</p></div></div>
    <div><div class="k">Why</div><div class="v"><p>The elected buffer is correct and empty. Nothing in Stray opts into CustomDepth by default. The buffer only becomes a segmentation map if we ask objects to render into it.</p></div></div>
    <div><div class="k">How</div><div class="v"><p>Read-modify-write the masked bit, on the game thread, via the ProcessEvent queue — then verify.</p></div></div>
    <div><div class="k">Result</div><div class="v"><p>It took three failures to get from “writes verified” to “pixels on screen”.</p></div></div>
  </div>

  <div class="fail">
    <p class="hdr">Failure</p>
    <h5>64 writes verified, and the buffer still empty</h5>
    <dl>
      <dt>Symptom</dt><dd><p>64 primitives marked, 64 writes verified by read-back, CustomDepth target still <code>binds=0</code>. The writes were <em>correct</em> and did <em>nothing</em>.</p></dd>
      <dt>Cause</dt><dd>
        <p>The renderer does not read <code>bRenderCustomDepth</code> per frame. It reads an <code>FPrimitiveSceneProxy</code> built on the render thread.</p>
        <pre class="log">void UPrimitiveComponent::SetRenderCustomDepth(bool bValue) {
    if (bRenderCustomDepth != bValue) {
        bRenderCustomDepth = bValue;
        MarkRenderStateDirty();      // ← this is what we skipped
    }
}</pre>
      </dd>
      <dt>Fix</dt><dd><p>Find <code>SetRenderCustomDepth</code> as a <code>UFunction</code> in the class's <code>Children</code> chain and <strong>invoke it through ProcessEvent</strong> — asking the engine to do the thing rather than poking at its state. Which is exactly what the brief means by “hooking ProcessEvent to call engine functions safely on the game thread”.</p></dd>
    </dl>
  </div>

  <div class="fail">
    <p class="hdr">Fix that made things worse</p>
    <h5>Bounding the array walk cut coverage by 94%</h5>
    <dl>
      <dt>Change</dt><dd><p>Capped the marking pass at 3,000 objects, to avoid stalling the game thread.</p></dd>
      <dt>Result</dt><dd><p>Marked primitives went <strong>267 → 16</strong>.</p></dd>
      <dt>Cause</dt><dd><p>3,000 of ~350,000 slots is <strong>4%</strong> of the array, and the low indices are almost entirely engine bootstrap objects — <code>Class</code>, <code>Package</code>, <code>Function</code>. Renderable components live much further in.</p></dd>
      <dt>Real problem</dt><dd><p>I bounded the wrong thing. The array walk is cheap read-only CPU work. The expensive part is the two UFunction calls per match, which run inside <code>ProcessEvent</code>.</p></dd>
      <dt>Fix</dt><dd><p>Split them. <code>CollectCandidates</code> walks the whole array on any thread; <code>MarkBatch(n)</code> marks a bounded batch on the game thread.</p></dd>
    </dl>
  </div>

  <div class="fail">
    <p class="hdr">Failure — cost three runs</p>
    <h5>Photographing the buffer 38 seconds before anything was in it</h5>
    <dl>
      <dt>Symptom</dt><dd><p>Three consecutive runs concluded “CustomDepth doesn't work”: masks came back <code>distinct stencil values: 0</code> every time.</p></dd>
      <dt>Cause</dt><dd>
        <pre class="log">[segcap  3.125] mask frame 2 dumped ... distinct stencil values: 0
[segcap 41.250] marked 267 primitives</pre>
        <p><code>OnMaskReady</code> dumped only the first three frames it ever saw. Those landed at t=3.1 s. Marking did not happen until t=41.2 s.</p>
        <p><strong>Both lines were in every log.</strong> I read them repeatedly across three runs as separate facts and never as a sequence.</p>
      </dd>
      <dt>Fix</dt><dd><p>Dump on <strong>content</strong> rather than frame number, removing the timing coupling entirely: the capture happens when there is something to capture, whenever that turns out to be.</p></dd>
      <dt>Cost</dt><dd><p>Two <em>correct</em> fixes were written for hypotheses that were not the problem. The render-proxy staleness above was a real bug and the engine setters were the right call — but neither was why the mask was empty.</p></dd>
    </dl>
  </div>

  <div class="callout">
    <span class="tag">The shutter fired at the wrong moment three times</span>
    <p>This same shape recurred twice more later — once when the recording gate started on
    the first non-empty mask (before the working set filled), and once when a dense capture
    stride spent its whole budget in 1.6 seconds. In all three, the trigger condition was
    technically satisfied long before the thing it was meant to detect was actually
    happening.</p>
  </div>
</section>

<!-- ============================ 8 ============================ -->
<section id="c8">
  <h2>Chapter 8</h2>
  <span class="chapno">Identity in eight bits</span>
  <h3>255 slots against 32,836 markable primitives</h3>

  <p>This is the part of the brief that is a design problem rather than an engineering one:
  <em>“the obvious channel is only 8 bits; think about what an ID means across frames and how
  a mask joins back to a real game object.”</em></p>

  <div class="callout">
    <span class="tag">The core distinction</span>
    <p>A stencil slot is a <strong>lease</strong>, not an identity. 255 values cannot name
    33,000 objects. So the slot is recycled aggressively, and a separate <strong>64-bit
    stable id</strong> keyed on <code>(pointer, serialNumber)</code> is the actual identity.
    The per-frame sidecar is what joins them.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="diagram">
    <pre class="mermaid">
flowchart TD
  OBJ["UObject*<br/>+ GUObjectArray serial"] --> KEY["Key(pointer, serial)"]
  KEY --> SID["stableId : uint64<br/>allocated once, never reused"]
  SID --> LEASE{"visible now?"}
  LEASE -- yes --> SLOT["slot : uint8 (1..255)<br/>written into stencil"]
  LEASE -- "left the screen" --> REL["ReleaseSlot()<br/>stableId KEPT"]
  REL --> TRAIL["trailing binding<br/>(released: true)"]
  TRAIL -->|"slot reissued"| DROP["binding dropped"]
  SLOT --> SIDECAR["per-frame sidecar JSON<br/>slot → stableId, class, name"]
  TRAIL --> SIDECAR
  REL -.->|"object returns"| SLOT
    </pre>
  </div>

  <h4>Why the serial number is part of the key</h4>
  <p>UE recycles <code>GUObjectArray</code> slots after garbage collection, so a
  <code>UObject*</code> can be reused by a completely different object. Keying identity on
  the pointer alone would silently merge two objects into one track. The serial number
