  makes a recycled pointer a genuinely new identity, and the registry <em>counts</em> how
  often that happens so a hypothetical risk becomes a measured one.</p>

  <div class="fail">
    <p class="hdr">Failure</p>
    <h5>15,000 identities and 14,745 evictions in 150 seconds</h5>
    <dl>
      <dt>Symptom</dt><dd>
        <pre class="log">customdepth: marked 250 this batch (0 refused); 255 live slots,
             15000 identities, 14745 evictions</pre>
        <p>Reported every 250 ms, and it reads like progress.</p>
      </dd>
      <dt>Cause</dt><dd><p><code>markPass_</code> advanced once per <em>batch</em>, so the registry's “never evict something seen this pass” guard only ever protected the current 250. The next batch evicted all of them. The arithmetic was never survivable: ~38,000 primitives, 255 slots.</p></dd>
      <dt>Why it matters</dt><dd><p>Cycling does not label more of the scene. It guarantees no object holds an id long enough to be tracked across two frames — destroying the one property the identity registry exists to provide.</p></dd>
      <dt>Fix</dt><dd><p>Take only as many candidates as there are <em>free</em> slots. Evictions went to <strong>0</strong>.</p></dd>
    </dl>
  </div>

  <div class="fail">
    <p class="hdr">Failure — a perfectly healthy-looking metric</p>
    <h5>255 slots spent on objects nobody can see</h5>
    <dl>
      <dt>Symptom</dt><dd>
        <pre class="log">255 live slots, 0 evictions</pre>
        <p>Stable working set, zero churn. Every in-level mask still empty or containing one object.</p>
      </dd>
      <dt>Cause</dt><dd><p>The marker took the <em>first</em> 255 candidates it found. Against 32,836 markable primitives with a few hundred visible at any moment, essentially none were on screen. It had appeared to work at the main menu only because there were few enough objects there that some marked ones happened to be visible.</p></dd>
      <dt>Fix</dt><dd><p>Ask the engine. <code>UPrimitiveComponent::WasRecentlyRendered</code> had been sitting in the reflected function list since the first successful discovery run. Slots are now leased only to primitives the renderer actually drew, and <code>RefreshVisibility</code> hands them back when objects leave — so the 255-slot working set <em>follows the camera</em>.</p></dd>
      <dt>Detail that matters</dt><dd><p>Acquisition uses a 0.3 s tolerance and release 1.0 s. Deliberately unequal: with equal thresholds an object hovering at the edge of visibility acquires and releases a slot every pass, which is thrash by another name.</p></dd>
      <dt>Result</dt><dd><p>~23% of tested primitives visible at once; 60–143 distinct ids per mask; 86–98% of pixels labelled.</p></dd>
    </dl>
  </div>

  <div class="fail">
    <p class="hdr">Failure — the tool written to prove the claim reported that it was unproven</p>
    <h5>“Identity survives slot loss”: asserted by design, demonstrated by nothing</h5>
    <dl>
      <dt>Symptom</dt><dd>
        <pre class="log">2. slots that carried &gt;1 identity over the session: 14   ← recycling happens
3. identities that disappeared and came back      : 0
   identities that held more than one slot        : 0    ← never observed</pre>
      </dd>
      <dt>Diagnosis</dt><dd><p>Slot recycling <em>was</em> exercised, so the data looked like a real test. It was not: no object left and returned inside the 37-second captured window. The property was asserted by the design and demonstrated by nothing — inside a report that otherwise looked thorough.</p></dd>
      <dt>Fix 1</dt><dd><p>A unit test for <code>ReleaseSlot</code>, which had been added with the visibility work and had <strong>no coverage at all</strong> — eviction was tested, voluntary release was not. Eight new assertions, including: a returning object resumes its original stableId <em>under a different slot</em>, while the slot it used to hold now belongs to something else.</p></dd>
      <dt>Fix 2</dt><dd>
        <p>Capture stride widened so the observed window spans 150 s rather than 37 s. On the longer window:</p>
        <pre class="log">identities that disappeared and came back: 52
identities that held more than one slot  : 55

  id 26  slots 26,189,192   StaticMeshComponent0
  id 29  slots 29,191,194   StaticMeshComponent0</pre>
        <p>One object, three different pixel values across a session, one identity throughout.</p>
      </dd>
      <dt>Lesson</dt><dd><p>Check that the observation window contains the event you are claiming, before reporting that the event did not occur.</p></dd>
    </dl>
  </div>

  <div class="fail">
    <p class="hdr">Failure — found by the overlay, not by any log line</p>
    <h5>The sidecar described a different moment than its mask</h5>
    <dl>
      <dt>Symptom</dt><dd><p>A gameplay mask contained ids 154, 156, 242 and 255 with <strong>no binding at all</strong> in the sidecar written beside it — 5.4% of the frame labelled with an id whose meaning had already been recycled.</p></dd>
      <dt>Cause</dt><dd><p>Readback is asynchronous by design, and the marking thread continuously releases and re-leases slots. Reading the slot table when a mask <em>arrives</em> describes a different moment than the one that wrote its pixels.</p></dd>
      <dt>Fix</dt><dd><p>The marker publishes an immutable <code>shared_ptr</code> snapshot whenever the table changes — a few times a second, not per frame — and <code>Present</code> records which snapshot was live when it submitted each copy. Copying a pointer per frame is free; rebuilding a 250-entry table per frame would not have been.</p></dd>
      <dt>Residual, then fixed</dt><dd>
        <p>A primitive unmarked mid-frame can still write its old stencil value for a frame or two while the render proxy rebuilds. I estimated this as “small” and left it. Measured, it was 0.27% of pixels on a 37 s window and <strong>3.17%</strong> on a 150 s window — same defect, window too short to contain it.</p>
        <p><code>ReleaseSlot</code> now parks the binding in a <code>recentlyReleased_</code> map and the sidecar emits it flagged <code>"released": true</code> until the slot is reissued. Re-measured: <strong>0 unbound ids, 0.000% of labelled pixels</strong>, across 3,476 distinct ids over 76 masks.</p>
      </dd>
    </dl>
  </div>
</section>

<!-- ============================ 9 ============================ -->
<section id="c9">
  <h2>Chapter 9</h2>
  <span class="chapno">Removing the human</span>
  <h3>“It can't be done by a human in the future for production, right?”</h3>

  <p>Frank's reframing — from “produce a capture” to “produce a capture pipeline” — was the
  single most productive instruction in the project. Every remaining bug was found by the
  system running unattended for five minutes at a time. A human in the loop would have
  hidden all of them.</p>

  <div class="fail">
    <p class="hdr">Failure</p>
    <h5><code>SendInput</code> is delivered and ignored</h5>
    <dl>
      <dt>Symptom</dt><dd><p>Four scan-code Enter taps into Stray's menu. Nothing happened.</p></dd>
      <dt>Diagnosis</dt><dd><p>Proven, not assumed: the engine's object array stayed at the menu's 173,598 slots instead of growing to the ~320,000 an in-level session shows. The object count is an independent witness to whether the game changed state.</p></dd>
      <dt>Fix</dt><dd><p>ViGEmBus — a kernel-mode virtual gamepad bus. The game cannot distinguish it from real hardware. It also solved a second problem: a pad that <em>moves</em> generates varied scenes, and a static camera produces thousands of near-identical frames.</p></dd>
    </dl>
  </div>

  <div class="fail">
    <p class="hdr">Failure — the focus check asked the wrong question</p>
    <h5><code>GetForegroundWindow() == MainWindowHandle</code></h5>
    <dl>
      <dt>Symptom</dt><dd><p><code>window focused: False</code> on runs where the game was plainly in front.</p></dd>
      <dt>Cause</dt><dd><p>A fullscreen D3D12 title frequently has a <em>different</em> HWND in the foreground than the one .NET reports as <code>MainWindowHandle</code>. The focus was fine; the question was wrong.</p></dd>
      <dt>Fix</dt><dd><p>Compare owning <strong>PIDs</strong> — “is the game the active application” is the question that actually matters.</p></dd>
    </dl>
  </div>

  <div class="fail">
    <p class="hdr">Failure — the worst single error in the project</p>
    <h5>I diagnosed the user's machine instead of my instrument</h5>
    <dl>
      <dt>Symptom</dt><dd><p><code>foreground pid 0 = Idle</code>. I concluded the session was locked and told Frank so.</p></dd>
      <dt>Cause</dt><dd><p><code>GetForegroundWindow()</code> returns <code>NULL</code> transiently — notably during an exclusive-fullscreen mode switch, which is exactly what Stray does ~20 s after launch, precisely when the harness polled. <code>GetWindowThreadProcessId(NULL, ...)</code> yields 0, which I printed as “Idle”.</p></dd>
      <dt>Fix</dt><dd><p><code>HasForegroundWindow()</code> distinguishes “no foreground window at all” from “a window owned by PID 0”. The log now says <code>&lt;none - mid mode-switch&gt;</code>, and a null foreground is treated as <em>wait</em>, not <em>escalate</em>.</p></dd>
      <dt>Note</dt><dd><p>Verified afterwards that the automation process runs on <code>WinSta0\Default</code> and the API works correctly from it — the check I should have run <em>before</em> asserting anything about someone else's machine.</p></dd>
    </dl>
  </div>

  <div class="fail">
    <p class="hdr">Failure — four consecutive runs</p>
    <h5>The screensaver switches the input desktop</h5>
    <dl>
      <dt>Symptom</dt><dd><p><code>GetForegroundWindow()</code> returned NULL for 60 seconds straight, the gamepad was ignored, and every run stranded at the menu producing menu frames.</p></dd>
      <dt>False starts</dt><dd><p>I had already misdiagnosed this exact symptom twice — once as the mode switch above (plausible, it does return NULL), and once, worse, as a locked session.</p></dd>
      <dt>The measurement that settled it</dt><dd>
        <pre class="log">input desktop name : 'Screen-saver'      ← not 'Default'
screensaver running: True
screensaver timeout: 60 s
ScreenSaverIsSecure: 0                   ← NOT locked</pre>
      </dd>
      <dt>Cause</dt><dd><p>With nobody at the keyboard, Windows activates the screensaver after 60 s idle, which switches the <strong>input desktop</strong> from <code>Default</code> to <code>Screen-saver</code>. From <code>Default</code>, there genuinely is no foreground window any more.</p></dd>
      <dt>Why it took four runs</dt><dd><p><code>SetThreadExecutionState(ES_DISPLAY_REQUIRED)</code> — which the harness already called, and which I assumed covered this — prevents the display <em>powering down</em>. The screensaver is a separate mechanism. Necessary but not sufficient, and “I already handle that” is why it survived so long.</p></dd>
      <dt>Fix</dt><dd><p>Save and restore <code>SPI_GETSCREENSAVEACTIVE</code>, disable it for the run, and kill an already-running <code>scrnsave.scr</code> — disabling the setting does not dismiss one that is already up. Focus now lands at <strong>t=2 s</strong> every run.</p></dd>
      <dt>Three states, one symptom</dt><dd>
        <div class="scroll">
        <table>
          <thead><tr><th>State</th><th><code>OpenInputDesktop</code></th><th>Desktop name</th><th>Fix</th></tr></thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr><td>Mode switch in progress</td><td>succeeds</td><td><code>Default</code></td><td>wait</td></tr>
            <tr><td>Screensaver active</td><td>succeeds</td><td><code>Screen-saver</code></td><td>disable + dismiss</td></tr>
            <tr><td>Session locked</td><td><strong>denied</strong></td><td>—</td><td>nothing in user space</td></tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
        </div>
      </dd>
    </dl>
  </div>

  <h4>Closing the control loop</h4>
  <div class="loop">
    <div><div class="k">What</div><div class="v"><p>Make the pad react to whether the character is actually moving.</p></div></div>
    <div><div class="k">Why</div><div class="v"><p>The patrol was nine hardcoded steps on a cycle. It did not know where it was or that it had been walking into a wall for four minutes. An unattended run that wedges in a corner produces thousands of near-identical frames — worse than producing none, because it looks like data.</p></div></div>
    <div><div class="k">How</div><div class="v"><p>The sensor already existed. <code>segcap.dll</code> reads the pawn's world transform by reflection and publishes it in a shared memory block; <code>vpad</code> reads it and escalates through recovery behaviours — back up, back+turn, jump, turn 180 — when displacement stalls while movement is commanded.</p></div></div>
    <div><div class="k">Result</div><div class="v"><p>47–78 recoveries per run, and real traversal rather than circling. Distinct objects encountered per session went from <strong>~450 to 1,317</strong>.</p></div></div>
  </div>
  <p>Two design notes. The block is a <strong>seqlock</strong>, because the writer is the
  game thread and the reader is another process with no lock between them — a torn read
  would hand the agent a position that never existed, which as a stuck-detector input is
  worse than no reading, because it looks like motion. And ViGEm deliberately stays
  <em>out</em> of the game process: everything added to an injected DLL is risk taken on the
  game's behalf, and a 128-byte shared section costs the host nothing.</p>

  <div class="fail">
    <p class="hdr">Failure — the same shape as every timing bug in this project</p>
    <h5>The agent checked for the shared block once, at startup</h5>
    <dl>
      <dt>Symptom</dt><dd><p>First closed-loop run silently ran open-loop for its entire duration.</p></dd>
      <dt>Cause</dt><dd>
        <pre class="log">t+7.0s   vpad starts, OpenFileMapping fails
t+49.9s  segcap: publishing agent state</pre>
        <p>Perception cannot publish until ProcessEvent is verified and the engine layer has resolved. The agent announced its fallback exactly once, forty seconds before the thing it wanted appeared.</p>
      </dd>
      <dt>Fix</dt><dd><p>Retry every 2 s and attach mid-run.</p></dd>
    </dl>
  </div>

  <div class="fail">
    <p class="hdr">Crash — a data race present since the first commit</p>
    <h5>Two threads rebuilding the memory map 63 ms apart</h5>
    <dl>
      <dt>Symptom</dt><dd>
        <pre class="log">79.859  ue4: [t+60s] array has 331701 slots      ← discovery thread
79.922  ue4: 16459 readable regions mapped       ← marking thread
&lt;dead&gt;</pre>
      </dd>
      <dt>Cause</dt><dd>
        <p><code>g_readable</code>, the committed-memory map <code>IsReadable</code> binary-searches, was a bare global vector rebuilt in place — <code>clear()</code> then <code>push_back()</code> — while other threads searched it. <code>IsReadable</code> runs on the game thread on every marking write, on the discovery thread millions of times per scan, and on the render thread.</p>
      </dd>
      <dt>Precision about the mistake</dt><dd><p>I did not introduce the bug when I added the marking thread; I introduced the <em>conditions that exposed it</em>. The unsafe publication had been in the file since the first discovery run, reviewed several times, and I never read it as shared state because only one thread happened to write it.</p></dd>
      <dt>Fix</dt><dd><p>Publish the map as an immutable snapshot behind a <code>shared_mutex</code>: the builder fills a fresh vector off to the side and swaps it in under an exclusive lock; readers hold a <code>shared_ptr</code> for the duration of their search.</p></dd>
      <dt>Lesson</dt><dd><p>Re-audit shared state when you add a thread, not when it crashes.</p></dd>
    </dl>
  </div>
</section>

<!-- ============================ 10 ============================ -->
<section id="c10">
  <h2>Chapter 10</h2>
  <span class="chapno">Proving it is right</span>
  <h3>“A number in a log is not evidence”</h3>

  <h4>Layer 1 — ground truth on a fixture</h4>
  <p>The <code>d3d12_testapp</code> validator asserts all 16 quads carry their expected
  stencil ID at their expected pixel: 16 regions, 28,224 pixels each, exact centroids. The
  correct answer is known independently of the thing being tested.</p>

  <h4>Layer 2 — overlay on real gameplay</h4>
  <p>Colours come from golden-ratio hue stepping rather than a random palette, because
  adjacent ids are common between neighbouring objects and two similar greens touching each
  other look like one object. Id 0 renders <strong>fully transparent</strong> rather than
  black — painting it black would hide misalignment, and edge alignment is exactly what the
  tool exists to check.</p>

  <h4>Layer 3 — did we change what the player sees?</h4>
  <div class="loop">
    <div><div class="k">What</div><div class="v"><p>Detect whether enabling CustomDepth marking altered the rendered image.</p></div></div>
    <div><div class="k">Why</div><div class="v"><p>CustomDepth is an off-screen pass and <em>should</em> be invisible — unless a post-process samples it, which some games do for outlines. That is exactly the case worth detecting.</p></div></div>
    <div><div class="k">How</div><div class="v">
      <p>The naive test fails. Stray uses temporal AA: with a completely static camera, <strong>12.2% of pixels differ</strong> between two consecutive frames. Judged against zero, the test reports a visual change every single time.</p>
      <p>So the game's own frame-to-frame variation is measured first and used as the noise floor. Design detail: one run with marking toggled partway, not two separate runs — across sessions the cat's idle animation and the NPCs sit at different phases, a difference that has nothing to do with CustomDepth.</p>
    </div></div>
    <div><div class="k">Result</div><div class="v">
      <pre class="log">noise floor (off vs off) : mean 0.043, 12.2% of pixels differ, max 1
off vs on                : mean 0.045, 12.7% of pixels differ, max 2
ratio                    : 1.04x the noise floor  → PASS</pre>
    </div></div>
  </div>

  <h4>Layer 4 — are the labels <em>correct</em>, not just consistent?</h4>
  <p>Everything above proves the labels are consistent, decodable and stable. None of it
  proves slot 71's pixels are the object the sidecar names. A bug writing a
  consistent-but-wrong stencil value would pass all of it.</p>
  <p><code>verify_labels.py</code> tests three properties a wrong label breaks: a stableId
  must always name the same object; a real object projects to a mostly-connected region;
  and across 0.1 s an object should move roughly as much as the rest of the scene, because
  that is the camera.</p>

  <div class="fail">
    <p class="hdr">Failure — the validator's first run failed, and both failures were mine</p>
    <h5>“13,088 pixels in 13,088 pieces”</h5>
    <dl>
      <dt>Symptom</dt><dd><p>Regions where every single pixel was its own connected component.</p></dd>
      <dt>Cause</dt><dd><p>Not fragmentation — a <strong>stipple</strong>. UE4 renders dithered LOD transitions and dithered opacity as a screen-door pattern, and CustomDepth inherits it. Counting raw components called a perfectly well-formed label “completely fragmented”.</p></dd>
      <dt>Fix</dt><dd><p>A 3×3 morphological close, with the raw count kept and reported separately — dithering is a genuine constraint of the CustomDepth route, worth naming rather than silently repairing. Measured at 0.2–1.0% of regions.</p></dd>
    </dl>
  </div>

  <div class="fail">
    <p class="hdr">Failure — measuring my own statistic's instability</p>
    <h5>An object “moving 156× the scene”</h5>
    <dl>
      <dt>Symptom</dt><dd><p>One object flagged as teleporting, at 156× the frame's median displacement.</p></dd>
      <dt>Cause</dt><dd><p>It was a modular mesh whose bounding box was the <em>entire frame</em> in 4–5 pieces. As the camera panned, different pieces dominated and the whole-region centroid slid across the screen far faster than any individual piece moved.</p></dd>
      <dt>Fix</dt><dd><p>Track the largest blob's centroid, and skip regions that are not predominantly one blob. Then a third condition: flag only if the <em>absolute</em> displacement is also large — without it, a character walking across a static shot divides by a near-zero scene median and produces a huge ratio for entirely normal behaviour.</p></dd>
    </dl>
  </div>

  <p>Three transitions still survived, all real and unexplained — until the <em>action
  log</em> settled it in one query: right stick at ±16000, full deflection, the patrol's
  turn-in-place step. Under a fast yaw, perspective sweeps objects near the screen edges
  many times further in pixels than objects near the centre. The input recording had been
  added for world-model training and paid for itself first as a debugging instrument. The
  validator now prints stick deflection beside every flagged transition.</p>

  <div class="callout">
    <span class="tag">Stated limit</span>
    <p>These checks are <strong>necessary, not sufficient</strong>. A label wrong in a
    spatially <em>and</em> temporally coherent way — two objects that always move together
    and are always adjacent — would still pass. True ground truth needs intervention:
    unmark one primitive and confirm exactly its pixels vanish. That is a live-run test and
    it is not built.</p>
  </div>
</section>

<!-- ============================ 11 ============================ -->
<section id="c11">
  <h2>Chapter 11</h2>
  <span class="chapno">Serialization</span>
  <h3>One indexed file, and why the compressor is not in the DLL</h3>

  <div class="loop">
    <div><div class="k">What</div><div class="v"><p>Bundle a session — masks, colour frames, sidecars, actions — into one self-describing container with lossless compression, on the same frame grid as the video.</p></div></div>
    <div><div class="k">Why</div><div class="v"><p>A mask without its sidecar is undecodable: slot 42 is a different object in different frames. The format should make separating them impossible, not merely discouraged.</p></div></div>
    <div><div class="k">How</div><div class="v">
      <pre class="log">magic     8 bytes   "SEGCAP01"
hdrlen    u32
header    utf-8 JSON  {width, height, codec, records, frames}
records   ...         type u8, frame u64, rawlen u32, complen u32, payload
index     utf-8 JSON  [{type, frame, offset, rawlen, complen}, ...]
idxlen    u32
footer    8 bytes   "SEGCAPIX"</pre>
      <p>The index sits at the <strong>end</strong>, length in the last 12 bytes, so a reader can seek to any frame without scanning and the writer never needs to know the layout in advance — the same reason zip puts its directory last.</p>
    </div></div>
    <div><div class="k">Result</div><div class="v">
      <div class="scroll">
      <table>
        <thead><tr><th></th><th class="num">raw</th><th class="num">packed</th><th class="num">ratio</th></tr></thead>
        <tbody>
          <tr><td>masks</td><td class="num">663.6 MB</td><td class="num">9.9 MB</td><td class="num"><strong>66.7×</strong></td></tr>
          <tr><td>colour frames</td><td class="num">1940.9 MB</td><td class="num">937.6 MB</td><td class="num">2.1×</td></tr>
          <tr><td>sidecars</td><td class="num">11.2 MB</td><td class="num">0.8 MB</td><td class="num">13.9×</td></tr>
          <tr><td>total</td><td class="num">2615.6 MB</td><td class="num">948.4 MB</td><td class="num">2.8×</td></tr>
        </tbody>
      </table>
      </div>
      <p>Reported separately on purpose. Masks are 8-bit indexed images with large flat regions — close to the best case for a dictionary coder. Colour frames are photographic and barely compress. A single “2.8×” would hide both facts.</p>
    </div></div>
  </div>

  <h4>Why compression is in the tool, not the DLL</h4>
  <p>The capture path runs inside someone else's process, on the thread that presents
  frames. Everything on it has been kept to the minimum that cannot be done later: a GPU
  copy on the game's own queue, a fence poll, a memcpy out of a mapped buffer. Linking a
  compressor in there would add third-party code to a shipped game's address space and CPU
  time to its present loop, to save disk that is not scarce. Compression is a pure function
  of bytes already written; it belongs outside.</p>

  <h4>Two properties enforced in code rather than documented</h4>
  <ul>
    <li><strong>Lossless is verified, not asserted.</strong> <code>--verify</code>
    decompresses every record and byte-compares it against the file it came from —
    <strong>952/952 identical</strong>. A compression bug corrupting one frame in a thousand
    would otherwise surface as a mysteriously bad training example months later.</li>
    <li><strong>A mask cannot be packed without its sidecar.</strong> The packer refuses the
    whole container if any mask lacks one.</li>
  </ul>

  <h4>Actions, for world models</h4>
  <p>A world model learns <code>P(next frame | frame, action)</code>, so the input is
  recorded alongside the frames. The unusual property here is that the pipeline
  <em>synthesises</em> the input, so the action is known exactly rather than inferred — no
  hook into the game's input handling, no deadzone guessing, no sampling race.</p>
  <p>The cross-process join needed care: <code>vpad.exe</code> and the injected DLL are
  different processes, so anything process-relative cannot be compared. Both stamp
  <code>GetSystemTimeAsFileTime</code>. The frame stamp is taken at <strong>Present</strong>,
  not when the readback lands, or every action label would be several frames late. The join
  is a step function, because that is what a gamepad is — interpolating would invent stick
  positions the game never saw. Measured: <strong>300/300 frames matched to an
  action</strong>.</p>
</section>

<!-- ============================ 12 ============================ -->
<section id="c12">
  <h2>Chapter 12</h2>
  <span class="chapno">Generalisation</span>
  <h3>Does any of this survive a different engine?</h3>

  <p>Everything above was measured on one title, and the renderable allowlist literally
  contained <code>ToyoSplineMeshComponent</code> — Stray's internal prefix. Generalisation
  was the weakest claim in the project, so it was tested against <strong>inZOI</strong>:
  UE5, D3D12-only, 287 MB shipping binary. Staged, and read-only until explicitly cleared.</p>

  <div class="scroll">
  <table>
    <thead><tr><th>Layer</th><th>Carried over?</th><th>Evidence</th></tr></thead>
    <tbody>
      <tr><td>Injection</td><td><span class="chip ok">yes</span></td><td>verified loaded in a 287 MB UE5 process</td></tr>
      <tr><td>D3D12 hooking &amp; election</td><td><span class="chip ok">yes</span></td><td>0 descriptor misses across 451 targets; elects and holds a scene-res target</td></tr>
      <tr><td>GUObjectArray + FName</td><td><span class="chip ok">yes</span></td><td>found in 15 ms; 534,153 slots; 99.8% resolve rate</td></tr>
      <tr><td>Property reflection</td><td><span class="chip ok">after a fix</span></td><td>0 → <strong>153</strong> properties on <code>UPrimitiveComponent</code></td></tr>
      <tr><td>ProcessEvent discovery</td><td><span class="chip no">no</span></td><td>no UE5 answer; the probe crashed the game</td></tr>
    </tbody>
  </table>
  </div>

  <p><strong>I predicted the object array would break and it did not.</strong> UE5 changed a
  great deal about <code>FUObjectArray</code> and the name pool, and my written plan said so.
  It found both, because the search validates by <em>shape</em> rather than by
  version-specific patterns — a design choice made months earlier for a different reason
  that turned out to survive a whole engine major version.</p>

  <div class="fail">
    <p class="hdr">Failure — a safety claim that was not true</p>
    <h5>“Census mode is read-only” — it wasn't, and it killed the game</h5>
    <dl>
      <dt>Symptom</dt><dd>
        <pre class="log">ue4: PE candidate 69 -&gt; 1169 valid, 506460 invalid (rejected)
ue4: PE candidate 70 -&gt;  810 valid, 432080 invalid (rejected)
&lt;dead&gt;</pre>
      </dd>
      <dt>Cause</dt><dd><p>Finding ProcessEvent hooks UObject vtable slots 60–80 one at a time and calls whatever occupies each with ProcessEvent's signature. On UE4 that converges on slot 68 with a 4:1 ratio. On UE5 the ratios are 1169:506460 — the probe was hooking hot functions that are not ProcessEvent.</p></dd>
      <dt>The honest part</dt><dd><p>I described the run as read-only and it was not. Census mode suppressed GPU work and UObject writes — and never gated vtable hooking, because when it was written those were the only mutations worth thinking about. <strong>The mode was doing most of what it promised, which is exactly why nobody noticed it was not doing all of it.</strong></p></dd>
      <dt>Fix</dt><dd><p>Census mode now returns before ProcessEvent discovery and says so in the log.</p></dd>
    </dl>
  </div>

  <h4>The UE5 reflection fix, in three steps</h4>
  <p>Every class returned zero properties, which killed marking entirely — no
  <code>bRenderCustomDepth</code>, no masks. Rather than guess a new constant, it was
  measured.</p>

  <h5>Step 1 — dump the struct, side by side with Stray</h5>
  <div class="scroll">
  <table>
    <thead><tr><th>offset</th><th>Stray (UE4)</th><th>inZOI (UE5)</th></tr></thead>
    <tbody>
      <tr><td class="num">+0x40</td><td><code>SceneComponent</code> (SuperStruct)</td><td><code>SceneComponent</code> — same</td></tr>
      <tr><td class="num">+0x48</td><td><code>WasRecentlyRendered</code> (Children)</td><td><code>WasRecentlyRendered</code> — same</td></tr>
      <tr><td class="num">+0x50</td><td>ptr → decodes <code>MinDrawDistance</code></td><td>ptr → decodes <strong>nothing</strong></td></tr>
    </tbody>
  </table>
  </div>
  <p><code>ChildProperties</code> is at the same offset and <em>is</em> a valid pointer. The
  chain is there. What moved is the layout <em>inside</em> <code>FField</code>.</p>

  <h5>Step 2 — try every offset and print what decodes</h5>
  <pre class="log">name@+0x14 next@+0x18 -&gt; 8 links: NavAvoidanceMask, NavAvoidanceMask, NavAvoidanceMask...
name@+0x20 next@+0x18 -&gt; 8 links: MinDrawDistance, LDMaxDrawDistance,
                                  CachedMaxDrawDistance, DepthPriorityGroup</pre>
  <p>The second row is the answer — the same four properties, in the same order, as Stray's
  UE4 dump. <strong>UE5 shifted <code>FField</code> back 8 bytes:</strong>
  <code>NamePrivate</code> 0x28 → 0x20, <code>Next</code> 0x20 → 0x18.</p>
  <p>The first row matters just as much. It decoded eight links, so a test that counted
  successful decodes would have <em>accepted</em> it — but every link is the same name.
  Printing the decoded sample rather than a count is what exposed it.</p>

  <h5>Step 3 — calibrate at runtime, don't swap one constant for another</h5>
  <p><code>CalibrateFieldLayout()</code> runs once after discovery on every session, tries
  the candidates against classes known to have properties, and keeps whichever yields the
  most <strong>distinct</strong> names. UE4 values remain the default, so a build it cannot
  calibrate behaves exactly as before. The same delta is applied to the
  <code>FProperty</code> fields that follow the header, since the struct moved as a unit.</p>
  <pre class="log">ue4: field layout calibrated: name@+0x20 next@+0x18
     (12 distinct names; shift -8 vs UE4.25-4.27)
introspect: --- PrimitiveComponent : 153 reflected properties ---
introspect:   +0x0271  1  BoolProperty  bRenderCustomDepth
introspect:   +0x02A4  4  IntProperty   CustomDepthStencilValue</pre>
  <p>Both marking properties located on UE5, at completely different offsets from Stray's
  (<code>+0x216</code> mask <code>0x40</code>, and <code>+0x220</code>) — <em>by name</em>,
  which is the entire reason this is done by reflection.</p>
  <p><strong>Checked, not assumed:</strong> a full Stray run after the change gave 201 masks
  / 200 frames / 201 sidecars, <code>bRenderCustomDepth</code> still at the unchanged
  <code>+0x216 mask 0x40</code>, and label verification passing with 0 identities renamed.</p>
</section>

<!-- ============================ 13 ============================ -->
<section id="c13">
  <h2>Chapter 13</h2>
  <span class="chapno">Learning a game's controls</span>
  <h3>“Don't hardcode the operation. It's stupid.”</h3>

  <p>Frank's correction, and he was right — hardcoding had already been wrong twice on inZOI
  in a single session.</p>
  <ul>
    <li>First it assumed Stray's menu flow (A ×3) on a game whose menu is <em>mouse-driven
    and has nothing selected until a pad input arrives</em>. Those presses landed in live
    gameplay, and one of them opened an external browser to the game's news page — which is
    what had been “exiting” the game.</li>
    <li>Then it assumed the game's own on-screen legend was true. The legend says
    <em>“LB + R Move Camera”</em>. An empirical probe measured <strong>no effect at
    all</strong> from that combination.</li>
  </ul>

  <div class="loop">
    <div><div class="k">What</div><div class="v"><p>Discover a title's control scheme by measurement.</p></div></div>
    <div><div class="k">How</div><div class="v"><p><code>vpad --serve</code> holds the pad open and applies commands from a file, so the pad becomes an instrument something else can drive one input at a time. <code>probe_controls.py</code> presses each input and measures what changed on screen.</p></div></div>
    <div><div class="k">Result</div><div class="v">
      <pre class="log">RB + L stick forward     9.0x drift floor   run
L stick forward          3.6x               walk
LB + R stick            &lt;0.6x               nothing, despite the legend
everything else         &lt;1.6x               indistinguishable from drift</pre>
    </div></div>
  </div>

  <h4>Three things that make it honest rather than confident</h4>
  <ol>
    <li><strong>A drift floor.</strong> A living game is never still — inZOI idles at ~8.7
    mean-abs on a downscaled frame with samples ranging 2 to 12. Measured between every
    probe. Without it, every button “works”. Same principle as the TAA noise floor.</li>
    <li><strong>A foreground guard.</strong> It screenshots a <em>region</em>, so anything
    covering it gets measured instead. On the first run, A opened a browser and twelve
    consecutive probes confidently reported “no visible effect” — about a static webpage.
    It now verifies the game owns the foreground before each probe and <em>stops</em> rather
    than emitting rows about whatever is on top.</li>
    <li><strong>Recovery between probes.</strong> If a change persisted, press B and verify
    the frame returns. Whether it worked is recorded, not assumed — and it classifies for
    free: B undoes it → a menu; B doesn't → you actually moved.</li>
  </ol>

  <h4>Entering gameplay, discovered one observed step at a time</h4>
  <pre class="log">D-pad Down  →  takes gamepad focus, "Continue" highlights
A           →  Load panel, first slot preselected
A           →  loads
~60s        →  loading screen
X           →  EXIT UI FOCUS   ← nothing would have guessed this</pre>
  <p>The game lands in <strong>UI Focus mode</strong> with the minimap focused, and until X
  is pressed every gameplay input is swallowed by the widget. That also retroactively
  explains the probe result above: the session where <code>LB + R stick</code> measured
  nothing was sitting in UI Focus, where the input genuinely does nothing. The measurement
  was honest; generalising it to “this input does nothing” was not.</p>
  <div class="callout">
    <span class="tag">Open item</span>
    <p>The probe records what it measured but not <em>what mode the game was in</em>, so its
    rows are only valid for a state nobody wrote down. That is the next thing to fix in it.</p>
  </div>
</section>

<!-- ============================ 14 ============================ -->
<section id="c14">
  <h2>Chapter 14</h2>
  <span class="chapno">Where it stands</span>
  <h3>Results, limitations, and what I would do next</h3>

  <h4>Measured</h4>
  <div class="scroll">
  <table>
    <thead><tr><th>Property</th><th class="num">Measured</th><th>Tool</th></tr></thead>
    <tbody>
      <tr><td>Objects per mask</td><td class="num">47 – 143</td><td><code>overlay.py</code></td></tr>
      <tr><td>Pixels labelled</td><td class="num">86 – 98.1%</td><td>largest single region averages 41%</td></tr>
      <tr><td>Mask ids with no sidecar binding</td><td class="num">0</td><td><code>identity_report.py</code></td></tr>
      <tr><td>Slot ambiguity within a frame</td><td class="num">0</td><td><code>identity_report.py</code></td></tr>
      <tr><td>Identities that changed what they name</td><td class="num">0 of 448</td><td><code>verify_labels.py</code></td></tr>
      <tr><td>Region is one connected blob</td><td class="num">median 1.000</td><td><code>verify_labels.py</code></td></tr>
      <tr><td>Objects moving against the scene</td><td class="num">0 of 1,850</td><td><code>verify_labels.py</code></td></tr>
      <tr><td>Identity survives slot loss</td><td class="num">52 returned, 55 multi-slot</td><td><code>identity_report.py</code></td></tr>
      <tr><td>Player-visible change</td><td class="num">1.04×</td><td><code>ab_diff.py</code></td></tr>
      <tr><td>Mask compression, lossless</td><td class="num">66.7×</td><td><code>pack.py --verify</code>, 952/952</td></tr>
      <tr><td>Frames matched to an action</td><td class="num">300 / 300</td><td>wall-clock join</td></tr>
      <tr><td>Descriptor misses</td><td class="num">0</td><td>injection precedes first D3D call</td></tr>
      <tr><td>Unit assertions</td><td class="num">25</td><td><code>test_identity.exe</code>, no game needed</td></tr>
    </tbody>
  </table>
  </div>

  <figure>
    <img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," alt="A frame from the demo video: rendered frame on the left, labelled segmentation on the right, with a controller state panel underneath.">
    <figcaption>
      A frame of the demo video. Rendered frame left, labelled mask right — the same frame
      by construction, both copied during the same Present call, so there is no
      synchronisation step and nothing to drift. Names come from that frame's own sidecar.
      The panel underneath is the controller state recorded with every frame, joined by
      wall clock across two processes.
    </figcaption>
  </figure>

  <h4>Limitations, stated rather than buried</h4>
  <ul>
    <li><strong>One GPU fault is unattributed.</strong> An early run ended with an
    <code>nvlddmkm</code> timeout inside it. The obvious suspect — readback rate — does not
    fit, since identical rates completed 9,300 submissions in other runs, and it has not
    recurred in fifteen runs since.</li>
    <li><strong>Correctness is statistical, not ground truth.</strong> A label wrong in a
    spatially <em>and</em> temporally coherent way would pass every check.</li>
    <li><strong>“98% labelled” is softer than it sounds.</strong> The largest single region
    averages 41% of the frame. Excluding it, coverage is about 53%.</li>
    <li><strong>Object names are mostly non-unique engine defaults.</strong>
    <code>SkeletalMeshComponent0</code> appears ~33 times per frame as 33 different
    components. Solid <em>instance</em> identity, coarse semantics.</li>
    <li><strong>255 simultaneous objects</strong> — the channel width, structural rather than
    an implementation limit.</li>
    <li><strong>Instanced meshes never exercised on Stray.</strong> One component
    representing many visual instances would receive one id. inZOI has 837 of them.</li>
    <li><strong>Nanite untouched</strong>, and <strong>no D3D11 path</strong> — both
    deliberate, both real gaps against the brief.</li>
  </ul>

  <h4>What I would do next, in order</h4>
  <ol>
    <li><strong>The intervention test.</strong> Static camera, unmark exactly one primitive,
    confirm exactly its pixels vanish. Converts correctness from statistical to ground truth.
    About an hour.</li>
    <li><strong>Finish UE5.</strong> Reflection now works on inZOI, so the remaining wall is
    a safe <code>ProcessEvent</code> search — signature-based rather than brute-force slot
    probing, which killed the game once.</li>
    <li><strong>Derive renderability from the class hierarchy</strong> instead of a hardcoded
    allowlist, removing the last title-specific strings.</li>
    <li><strong>Continuous capture.</strong> The agent explores for 260 s and only 30 s is
    photographed.</li>
    <li><strong>Objective-following agent.</strong> <code>ProcessEvent</code> already sees
    every <code>UFunction</code> the game invokes — the game narrating its own events. A
    call histogram diffed between “in front of an interactable” and “in a corridor” would
    identify prompts without any vision at all.</li>
  </ol>
</section>

<section>
  <h2>Closing</h2>
  <p class="lede">The single most useful habit in this project was asking, before trusting a
  number: <strong>“what would this look like if the thing I am claiming were false?”</strong>
  If the answer is “the same”, the metric is not evidence.</p>
  <p>Every headline failure here passed that test only in retrospect.
  <code>marked 250 this batch</code>, <code>255 live slots, 0 evictions</code>,
  <code>21 masks captured</code>, <code>identities that came back: 0</code>,
  <code>writes stencil: no</code> — all true, all describing failures, none of them throwing
  an exception. The fix was never cleverness. It was making the instrument show its work, or
  finding a second independent way to ask the same question.</p>
</section>

  <p class="eyebrow">Take-home · originlab.ai</p>
  <h1>Per-pixel object IDs, extracted live from a shipped game</h1>
  <p class="standfirst">
    An injected DLL that pulls a segmentation map out of <em>Stray</em> while it runs —
    every pixel carrying the identity of the game object that drew it, on the same frame
    grid as the video. No source, no symbols, debug names stripped.
  </p>
  <p class="byline">
    <span>Target: Stray · UE4 · D3D12 · retail Steam build</span>
    <span>55 commits</span>
    <span>6,579 lines C++ · 3,972 lines tooling</span>
  </p>
</header>

<div class="stats">

<section>
  <h2>The ask</h2>
  <blockquote>
    <p>“Build a system that extracts a segmentation map on top of the video stream of a
    game, per-pixel object IDs, aligned with the rendered frames… I’d rather see two or
    three explored properly than all of them skimmed.”</p>
    <p>Most interested in: a short video of masks over real gameplay; how you diagnosed
    things when they didn’t work — <em>the debugging story matters more to me than the
    final coverage number</em>; and where you used AI effectively, and where you had to
    override it.</p>
  </blockquote>
  <p class="lede">
    All three are delivered. This report leads with the scorecard, then spends most of its
    length on the second one, because that is what was asked for.
  </p>
</section>

<section>
  <h2>The result</h2>
  <figure>
    <img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," alt="A Stray gameplay frame with its per-pixel segmentation mask overlaid. The cat, a robot NPC, tree foliage, building faces and steps are each rendered in a distinct colour.">
    <figcaption>
      One captured frame at 1920×1080. 143 distinct object ids, 98.1% of pixels labelled.
      The cat is separated from the step it stands on; the robot NPC from the tree behind
      it; each building face is its own object. The speckle on the foliage is real — UE4
      renders dithered LOD transitions as a screen-door stipple and CustomDepth inherits
      it (see §7.14).
    </figcaption>
  </figure>
  <figure>
    <img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," alt="A frame from the demo video: rendered frame on the left, labelled segmentation on the right, with a controller state panel underneath.">
    <figcaption>
      A frame of the demo video. Rendered frame left, labelled mask right — the same frame
      by construction, both copied during the same Present call, so there is no
      synchronisation step and nothing to drift. Object names come from the frame's own
      sidecar. The panel underneath is the controller state recorded with every frame.
    </figcaption>
  </figure>
</section>

      </tbody>
    </table>
  </div>
  <p><strong>The A/B number needs its context.</strong> With a completely static camera,
  Stray's temporal AA still changes <strong>12.2% of pixels</strong> between two
  consecutive frames. Judged against zero, that test reports a visual change every single
  time regardless of what you did. The noise floor <em>is</em> the measurement; 1.04× of it
  is the result.</p>
</section>

<section>
  <h2>The debugging story</h2>
  <p class="lede">
    Roughly two thirds of the time lost on this project went to a single failure mode:
    <strong>a measurement that could not observe the thing it was being used to judge,
    reporting the answer that matched the current hypothesis.</strong> Not one of them
    threw an exception. Five of the worst follow; the full catalogue is
    <code>docs/DEBUGGING.md</code>, which runs to fifteen entries.
  </p>

  <div class="bug">
    <h4>The census said the game had no depth buffer</h4>
    <span class="cost">cost: one run, plus a wrong conclusion about the engine</span>
    <p>In-level, the render-target census contained exactly one depth-stencil target: a
    1×1 dummy. Read literally that says a 3D game renders without depth — absurd, and the
    log stated it flatly.</p>
    <p>The census can only report targets it successfully <em>resolved</em>, so it cannot
    distinguish “absent” from “filtered out by me”. Logging every resource passed to
    <code>CreateDepthStencilView</code>, upstream of the filter, answered it in one run:</p>
    <div class="ev">
      <span class="tag">segcap.log</span>
      <pre>CreateDSV #2: R32G8X24_TYPELESS 640x360 ... D32_FLOAT_S8X24_UINT
CreateDSV #5: R32G8X24_TYPELESS 640x360
CreateDSV #6: R32G8X24_TYPELESS 640x360</pre>
    </div>
    <p>They were 640×360 against a 1280×720 backbuffer, because the game was configured
    with <code>ScreenPercentage=50</code>. The election hard-required backbuffer
    dimensions. That rule was never sound — screen percentage, dynamic resolution and
    upsampling are all normal. It was replaced with “matches the backbuffer's aspect ratio
    and is the largest of that shape”, which later let the whole election work
    <em>unchanged</em> on a second game rendering at 1280×800 into a 2560×1600 backbuffer.
    A bug fixed properly generalised; a magic number would not have.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="bug">
    <h4>255 slots spent on objects nobody can see</h4>
    <span class="cost">cost: two runs, and a metric that looked perfect throughout</span>
    <div class="ev">
      <span class="tag">what the log said</span>
      <pre>customdepth: 255 live slots, 0 evictions</pre>
      <p>Healthy. It was describing 255 labels on objects that were off screen.</p>
    </div>
    <p>The marker took the first 255 candidates it found. Against 32,836 markable
    primitives with a few hundred visible at any moment, essentially none were on screen.
    It had <em>appeared</em> to work at the main menu only because there were few enough
    objects there that some marked ones happened to be visible.</p>
    <p>The fix was to stop guessing and ask the engine.
    <code>UPrimitiveComponent::WasRecentlyRendered</code> had been sitting in the reflected
    function list since the first successful discovery run. Slots are now leased only to
    primitives the renderer actually drew, and handed back when objects leave, so the
    255-slot working set follows the camera.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="bug">
    <h4>Four runs lost to a screensaver — and I blamed the user's machine</h4>
    <span class="cost">cost: four runs, and two confident wrong diagnoses</span>
    <p>Unattended runs kept stranding at the main menu.
    <code>GetForegroundWindow()</code> returned NULL for sixty seconds straight, the
    virtual gamepad's input went nowhere, and every capture was of a menu.</p>
    <p>I diagnosed it twice by inference and was wrong both times — once as an
    exclusive-fullscreen mode switch, which does transiently return NULL, and once, worse,
    as a locked session, which meant telling the user their machine was locked when it was
    not. They corrected me.</p>
    <div class="ev">
      <span class="tag">the measurement that settled it</span>
      <pre>input desktop name : 'Screen-saver'      &lt;- not 'Default'
screensaver running: True
screensaver timeout: 60 s
ScreenSaverIsSecure: 0                   &lt;- NOT locked</pre>
    </div>
    <p>With nobody at the keyboard, the screensaver activates and switches the
    <em>input desktop</em>. From <code>Default</code>, there genuinely is no foreground
    window any more. <code>ES_DISPLAY_REQUIRED</code>, which the harness already called and
    which I had assumed covered this, prevents display power-off — the screensaver is a
    separate mechanism. Necessary but not sufficient, and “I already handle that” is why it
    took four runs.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="bug">
    <h4>A claim with no evidence, caught by the tool written to prove it</h4>
    <span class="cost">cost: none — this one was caught before shipping</span>
    <p>The central identity claim is that a 64-bit stable id survives losing its 8-bit
    slot, so an object that goes off screen and returns resumes its own track rather than
    fragmenting into two. <code>identity_report.py</code> was written to demonstrate it on
    real data. It reported:</p>
    <div class="ev">
      <span class="tag">identity_report.py, 37-second window</span>
      <pre>slots that carried &gt;1 identity : 14   &lt;- recycling happens
identities that came back      : 0
identities that held &gt;1 slot   : 0    &lt;- never observed</pre>
    </div>
    <p>Slot recycling <em>was</em> exercised, so the data looked like a real test. It was
    not: no object left and returned inside that window. The property was asserted by the
    design and demonstrated by nothing, inside a report that otherwise looked thorough.</p>
    <p>Two fixes, for two different gaps. <code>ReleaseSlot</code> — added with the
    visibility work — had no unit test at all; eviction was covered, voluntary release was
    not. And the capture stride was widened so the observed window spans 150 seconds rather
    than 37. On the longer window:</p>
    <div class="ev">
      <span class="tag">same tool, 150-second window</span>
      <pre>identities that disappeared and came back: 52
identities that held more than one slot  : 55

  id 26  slots 26,189,192   StaticMeshComponent0</pre>
      <p>One object, three different pixel values across the session, one identity
      throughout. That is the 8-bit channel carrying stable identity, rather than a design
      document saying it does.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="bug">
    <h4>A data race that had been there since the first commit</h4>
    <span class="cost">cost: one crashed game, 80 seconds into a run</span>
    <div class="ev">
      <span class="tag">the last two lines before the process died</span>
      <pre>79.859  ue4: [t+60s] array has 331701 slots      &lt;- discovery thread
79.922  ue4: 16459 readable regions mapped       &lt;- marking thread</pre>
    </div>
    <p>Two threads, 63 ms apart, both rebuilding the committed-memory map that
    <code>IsReadable</code> binary-searches — a bare global vector, cleared and reallocated
    in place while other threads searched it.</p>
    <p>Worth being precise about the mistake: I did not introduce the bug when I added the
    marking thread, I introduced the <em>conditions that exposed it</em>. The unsafe
    publication had been in the file since the first discovery run, reviewed several times,
    and I never read it as shared state because only one thread happened to write it. Fixed
    by publishing the map as an immutable snapshot behind a <code>shared_mutex</code>.</p>
  </div>

  <h3>The pattern, and what actually caught these</h3>
  <p>Every one of these produced a plausible, confident, healthy-looking number:
  <code>marked 250 this batch</code>, <code>255 live slots, 0 evictions</code>,
  <code>21 masks captured</code>, <code>identities that came back: 0</code>. All true. All
  describing failures.</p>
  <p>The habit that helped was asking, before trusting a number,
  <strong>“what would this look like if the thing I am claiming were false?”</strong> — and
  if the answer is “the same”, the metric is not evidence. Concretely that became three
  rules, each of which is now enforced somewhere in the code:</p>
  <ul>
    <li>Any filter that can hide evidence needs a log line <em>upstream</em> of itself, or
    its silence is unreadable. This bug occurred twice, months apart.</li>
    <li>Pair every counter that only goes up with one that can go down.</li>
    <li>Check that the observation window contains the event you are claiming, before
    reporting that the event did not occur.</li>
  </ul>
</section>

<section>
  <h2>Dynamic vs PSO-baked state — why it decided the architecture</h2>
  <p>This bullet turned out not to be a detail. In D3D12, <code>StencilEnable</code>,
  <code>StencilWriteMask</code> and the pass/fail operations are all <strong>baked into the
  pipeline state object</strong>. The only dynamic piece is the reference value.</p>
  <p>So the obvious plan — hook every draw, set a per-object value, let it land in stencil —
  cannot work from an injected DLL. Making the game's draws write arbitrary ids requires
  building stencil-writing twins of every PSO the title uses, thousands of them, swapping
  them at <code>SetPipelineState</code> while keeping all other state byte-identical. That
  is a shadow renderer, not instrumentation, and every mismatch is a visual artifact in
  someone's game. Setting <code>OMSetStencilRef</code> alone accomplishes nothing when the
  bound PSO has <code>StencilEnable = FALSE</code>.</p>
  <p>Hence routing through UE's CustomDepth pass, which already has those PSOs and already
  feeds <code>CustomDepthStencilValue</code> to <code>OMSetStencilRef</code> per primitive.
  The intervention becomes setting an integer on a game object, and the D3D12 hooks stay
  strictly read-only — none alters an argument, none issues GPU work.</p>
  <p><strong>And it is why the id is 8 bits.</strong> Not a shortcut: it is the width of the
  pass the engine already runs. The 255-slot constraint the identity design works around is
  structural, imposed by where the line between instrumenting and rewriting falls.</p>
  <p>One honest consequence: <code>SetPipelineState</code> is deliberately not hooked, so
  the census knows which depth target was bound and how often, but not what stencil
  operation its draws were configured to perform. That is exactly why the election scores
  on bind count, clear count, format and persistence — the signals actually observable from
  dynamic state.</p>
</section>

<section>
  <h2>Does it generalise?</h2>
  <p>Everything above was measured on one title, and the renderable allowlist contained
  <code>ToyoSplineMeshComponent</code> — Stray's internal prefix. Generalisation was the
  weakest claim in the project, so it was tested against <strong>inZOI</strong>: UE5,
  D3D12-only, a 287 MB shipping binary. Every run read-only.</p>
  <div class="scroll">
    <table>
      <thead><tr><th>Layer</th><th>Carried over?</th><th>Evidence</th></tr></thead>
      <tbody>
        <tr><td>Injection</td><td><span class="chip ok">yes</span></td><td>verified loaded in a 287 MB UE5 process</td></tr>
        <tr><td>D3D12 hooking &amp; election</td><td><span class="chip ok">yes</span></td><td>0 descriptor misses across 451 targets; elects and holds a scene-res target</td></tr>
        <tr><td>GUObjectArray + FName</td><td><span class="chip ok">yes</span></td><td>found in 15 ms; 534,153 slots; 99.8% resolve rate</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Property reflection</td><td><span class="chip ok">after a fix</span></td><td>0 → <strong>153</strong> properties on <code>UPrimitiveComponent</code></td></tr>
        <tr><td>ProcessEvent discovery</td><td><span class="chip no">no</span></td><td>no UE5 answer; the probe crashed the game once</td></tr>
      </tbody>
    </table>
  </div>
  <p>The reflection fix is the interesting part. Every class returned zero properties, which
  killed marking entirely. Dumping the raw <code>UStruct</code> showed
  <code>ChildProperties</code> at the <em>same</em> offset and holding a valid pointer — the
  chain was there. So a probe walked every aligned offset inside the field and printed which
  ones decoded to readable names:</p>
  <div class="ev">
    <span class="tag">FField name-offset probe, inZOI</span>
    <pre>name@+0x14 next@+0x18 -> NavAvoidanceMask, NavAvoidanceMask, NavAvoidanceMask...
name@+0x20 next@+0x18 -> MinDrawDistance, LDMaxDrawDistance,
                         CachedMaxDrawDistance, DepthPriorityGroup</pre>
    <p>The second row is the answer — the same four properties, in the same order, as
    Stray's UE4 dump. UE5 shifted <code>FField</code> back 8 bytes.</p>
  </div>
  <p>The first row is why the probe prints samples rather than counts: it decoded eight
  links too, but every one is the same name. The calibration therefore scores on
  <em>distinct</em> names, runs once after discovery on every session, and keeps the UE4
  values as the default so a build it cannot calibrate behaves exactly as before. Result:
  <code>bRenderCustomDepth</code> and <code>CustomDepthStencilValue</code> are both located
  on UE5, at completely different offsets from Stray's — <em>by name</em>, which is the
  entire reason this is done by reflection.</p>
  <p>Checked, not assumed: a full Stray run after the change gave 201 masks / 200 frames /
  201 sidecars with <code>bRenderCustomDepth</code> still at the unchanged
  <code>+0x216 mask 0x40</code>.</p>
</section>

<section>
  <h2>Where AI helped, and where it was overridden</h2>
  <div class="two">
    <div>
      <h4>What it was genuinely good at</h4>
      <p>Boilerplate with a known shape — vtable hooking, the readback ring, COM plumbing —
      needed no correction.</p>
      <p>But the real payoff was <strong>instruments</strong>. Almost every hard bug here was
      found by a purpose-built tool rather than by reasoning: the election score table with
      rejection reasons, <code>CreateDSV</code> logging upstream of the census filter, the
      ProcessEvent valid/invalid ratio, <code>identity_report.py</code>,
      <code>ab_diff.py</code>'s noise floor.</p>
      <p>Writing a bespoke instrument is normally not worth the time. When that cost drops to
      a couple of minutes, the correct strategy shifts — measure far more aggressively than
      you otherwise would. That is a change in how to work, not just faster typing.</p>
    </div>
    <div>
      <h4>Where the human overrode it, and was right</h4>
      <p><strong>D3D11 vs D3D12.</strong> The initial recommendation was D3D11, and part of
      the argument was about appearances rather than engineering. That should not have been in
      the analysis. Frank rejected it: <em>“if there's a hardship then let's face it.”</em>
      D3D12 is strictly harder — the queue is not reachable from the swapchain, descriptor
      handles carry no identity, resource state must be shadowed — and every one of those maps
      onto a bullet in the brief.</p>
      <p><strong>“That frame is a menu.”</strong> Menu captures were presented as progress.
      They were real masks and not the deliverable. The rejection forced the work that
      uncovered three genuine bugs, none of which are visible at a menu.</p>
      <p><strong>“It can't be done by a human in future.”</strong> Reframed the target from
      “produce a capture” to “produce a capture pipeline”, which is what exposed the
      screensaver failure at all.</p>
      <p><strong>“Don't hardcode the controls.”</strong> Correct, and it had already been
      wrong twice on the second game.</p>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>

<section>
  <h2>Limitations, stated rather than buried</h2>
  <ul>
    <li><strong>One GPU fault is unattributed.</strong> An early run ended with an
    <code>nvlddmkm</code> timeout inside it. The obvious suspect — readback rate — does not
    fit, since identical rates completed 9,300 submissions in other runs, and it has not
    recurred in fifteen runs since. Logged as unexplained rather than explained away.</li>
    <li><strong>Correctness is statistical, not ground truth.</strong>
    <code>verify_labels.py</code> narrows the space of possible corruption considerably, but
    a label wrong in a spatially <em>and</em> temporally coherent way would still pass. The
    airtight version needs intervention: unmark one primitive, confirm exactly its pixels
    vanish. Not built.</li>
    <li><strong>“98% labelled” is softer than it sounds.</strong> The single largest region
    averages 41% of the frame — usually a wall. Excluding it, coverage is about 53%.</li>
    <li><strong>Object names are mostly non-unique engine defaults.</strong>
    <code>SkeletalMeshComponent0</code> appears ~33 times per frame as 33 different
    components. The pipeline gives solid <em>instance identity</em> and only coarse
    semantics.</li>
    <li><strong>255 simultaneous objects.</strong> The channel width, not an implementation
    limit — but a scene needing more would need a second channel or the Nanite route.</li>
    <li><strong>Instanced meshes never exercised on Stray.</strong> One component
    representing many visual instances would receive one id. inZOI has 837 of them.</li>
  </ul>
</section>

<section>
  <h2>What I would do next</h2>
  <ol>
    <li><strong>The intervention test</strong> — static camera, unmark exactly one
    primitive, confirm exactly its pixels disappear. Converts correctness from statistical
    to ground truth. About an hour.</li>
    <li><strong>Finish UE5</strong> — reflection now works on inZOI, so the remaining wall
    is a safe <code>ProcessEvent</code> search. The current one probes vtable slots and
    killed the game once; it needs a signature-based approach, not brute force.</li>
    <li><strong>Derive renderability from the class hierarchy</strong> rather than a
    hardcoded allowlist, removing the last title-specific strings.</li>
    <li><strong>Continuous capture</strong> — the agent explores for 260 s and only 30 s is
    photographed. For real collection the capture should not stop.</li>
  </ol>
</section>

## 60-second sanity check

```powershell
cd <repo>
.\build.ps1
.\build\bin\test_identity.exe                # expect: ALL PASSED (0 failures)
python tools\capture.py inzoi --preflight    # control flow, no game, ~1s
```

Run `--preflight` first. Four runs died to harness mistakes that surfaced only
when their line executed, four minutes in, each costing a loaded game world.

**The capture harness needs a python whose `ctypes` works.** `tools/harness.py`
is ctypes all the way down — process liveness, window handles, input — so an
interpreter with a broken `_ctypes` (a conda env missing libffi, for instance)
dies on an import three frames in. Find a working one with:

```powershell
python -c "import ctypes; import sys; print(sys.executable)"
& <that python> tools\capture.py ...
```

`capture.py` re-execs itself onto a working interpreter if the one you invoke it
with cannot import ctypes, so in practice this is self-healing; the note is here
because the error message reads as "the harness is broken" rather than "wrong
interpreter", and that has cost time more than once.

**The ANALYSIS tools need numpy, and it may not be the same interpreter.**
`overlay.py`, `verify_labels.py`, `identity_report.py` and `make_demo.py` import
numpy but use no ctypes, so they have the opposite requirement to the harness.
If your ctypes-capable python has no numpy, these fail with a bare
`ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'numpy'`, which reads as "the tool is
broken" rather than "wrong interpreter". Unlike `capture.py` they do not
re-exec.

One environment with both numpy and a working ctypes removes the split
entirely; `pip install numpy` into the harness's interpreter is the whole fix.
It is left as a note rather than done in a script, because installing packages
into someone's environment behind their back is not this project's business.

Then a real run:

```powershell
python tools\capture.py stray --seconds 300 --captures 300 --stride 6
python tools\capture.py inzoi --inject --seconds 200 --captures 400 --stride 8
```

Stray: expect `401 masks + 400 frames + 401 sidecars` and, in `build\bin\segcap.log`,
`readback submitted=N delivered=N-1 dropped=0`. **Those three numbers are the
health check for the Present path** — `delivered` tracking `submitted` one
behind, and `dropped` at zero. If `submitted` freezes at exactly 3 while
`dropped` climbs, the ring is full and nothing is completing; that is a
completion-test failure, not a copy failure, and §8.24 is the whole story.

inZOI: expect ~400 masks and these lines:

```
idbuf: FOUND OUR IDS in <ptr> channel G16(high) (100.0% of non-zero texels ...)
state: WORLD level=RedCity_Map sim=RUNNING objects=564553 delta=+0 marked=255
colour: FIRST backbuffer copy recorded
loaded world 'RedCity_Map' after 74s
```

inZOI dies during world streaming on roughly half of attempts. That is expected,
`--retries 3` is the default, and a run that reaches gameplay captures reliably.

Then:

```powershell
python tools\overlay.py build\bin\segcap_mask_<N>.pgm --sidecar build\bin\segcap_mask_<N>.json --out check.png
python tools\make_demo.py --dir build\bin --out demo.mp4
python tools\identity_report.py --dir build\bin
python tools\verify_labels.py --dir build\bin
```

If anything misbehaves, `docs\DEBUGGING.md` §7–8 almost certainly already
describes it.

## How inZOI works, in one page

This is the part worth not re-deriving.

**The ids are not in the stencil plane.** On UE 5.6 the Nanite CustomDepth export
takes the pixel-shader path — the compute path needs `GRHISupportsExplicitHTile`,
which is console-only — and that path writes depth to `CombinedCustomDepth` and
the stencil **value** to a separate **colour** target, `CombinedCustomStencil`,
of format `PF_R16G16_UINT` (`DXGI_FORMAT_R16G16_UINT` = **36**). The elected
depth-stencil's stencil plane is never written, which is why inZOI's first masks
were noise that nevertheless passed a structural check (§8.6).

The ids are in **channel G16**, the high half: `(word >> 16) & 0xFFFF`.

**It is found by measurement, not by assumption.** `hooks_idprobe.cpp` copies
candidate integer targets and asks one question: what fraction of non-zero texels
carry a stencil value we currently lease? Ours answers 100%. `segcap.idformat=36`
seeds the format so discovery is deterministic rather than a search.

Acceptance needs that fraction **and** enough distinct leased values to rule out
a coincidence — scaled to the leased set, an eighth of it. Do not reintroduce a
"no single value may exceed N% of the match" rule: inZOI's apartment shell is one
mesh covering 60–85% of an indoor view, and that rule rejected the correct buffer
on every run it was active. It is a fact about the room, not the buffer. §8.12.

**And the labels are verified by intervention, not by inspection.** Run with
`--groundtruth`: it unmarks one object mid-run and requires exactly that id's
pixels to vanish. Last verdict: 161,787 px → 0, no other id lost pixels. If you
change how slots are marked or evicted, re-run this — it is the only check that a
coherent-but-wrong mask cannot pass.

**Copies are recorded into the game's own command list, at the game's own
barrier** (`hooks_detours.cpp`), never issued from our queue at Present. Outside
an engine you cannot know a transient resource's current state; at the barrier
you can, because `StateBefore` comes out of the caller's struct where it is true
by construction. The same applies to the colour frame — the gate is any write
state → `PRESENT` on a registered backbuffer.

Two traps in that gate, both already paid for: `D3D12_RESOURCE_STATE_PRESENT`
is **0**, so `(state & PRESENT) == PRESENT` is vacuously true and looks like a
check; and `0x400` is `COPY_DEST`, not `RENDER_TARGET` (which is `0x4`) — inZOI
*copies* the DLSS-upscaled image into the backbuffer rather than rendering into
it, so a `RENDER_TARGET`-only gate never fires.

**8 bits is the ceiling.** 255 ids against ~560,000 objects. The budget is spent
by screen area: `NoteMaskCoverage` feeds per-slot pixel counts back to the
marker, which evicts slots labelling specks — but **only under pressure**, since
evicting whenever a slot looks small drained the pool from 255 to 57.
Instanced/foliage components are capped at a third of the budget, because one
`InstancedStaticMeshComponent` covers every instance of a mesh and will otherwise
eat the budget with ground and trees.

---

## What is still open

**THREE inZOI crash families, not two** — this section said two for weeks, until
they were counted instead of remembered (§8.16). Of twelve consecutive reports:
**nine** are `E_ABORT` from `ResizeBuffers` (`D3D12Viewport.cpp:554`), **one** is
the `E_INVALIDARG` from the game's own `Close()` (`D3D12CommandList.cpp:277`)
that had absorbed most of the effort, and **two** are access violations. Eight
candidate explanations are killed with evidence rather than left as guesses.

None blocks capture: the harness retries, and a run that reaches gameplay
captures reliably.

`Close()` is D3D12's deferred error point — recording methods return void and
rejections latch — so a crash with none of our frames on the stack is exactly
what our own bad copy looks like. A control run showed passive hooks surviving to
t=437 while marked runs died at 45–114s, which implicates marking, but the
mechanism is not identified.

**The access-violation family is diagnosed and fixed on STRAY** (§8.27, §8.28),
and it turned out to be two unrelated bugs wearing one exception code:

- a TOCTOU in the discovery scan — `IsReadable` is a `VirtualQuery`, true when
  asked and false by the time of the read, which no length check can fix. Now
  SEH-guarded, so a torn read skips a candidate instead of killing the process.
- a `UWorld` pointer captured into a queued game-thread callback and handed back
  to `UGameplayStatics` after the level had been torn down. The engine faulted,
  five frames above ours. Now resolved inside the callback.

**Whether inZOI's two access violations are the same two causes is UNVERIFIED.**
They share an exception code and a plausible mechanism; that is not evidence.
Re-run inZOI on the current build before claiming it.

**Whole-process suspend**, occasionally, cause unknown. Signature: every thread
in `Wait`/`Suspended` with suspend count exactly 1 and zero CPU. `ResumeThread`
returns the *previous* count, so attempting recovery is also the diagnosis;
`harness.resume_all_threads` does it.

**inZOI colour frames include the HUD**, because the copy happens at Present,
after UI compositing. The mask is unaffected. Copying before the UI pass fixes it.

**One id holds ~56% of the frame** — the apartment shell is a single
`StaticMeshComponent0`. Accurate, and it looks lazy. Sub-component labelling is
not expressible in CustomDepth: the stencil value is per primitive.

---

## Traps that already cost time — do not re-pay for them

- **A running game holds `segcap.dll`, so `build.ps1` fails at LINK, not at
  compile.** `LNK1104: cannot open file 'bin\segcap.dll'` means the game is still
  up. You do not have to close it: Windows refuses to *overwrite* a mapped image
  but happily *renames* it, so `Rename-Item build\bin\segcap.dll segcap.dll.old`
  (and the `.pdb`) frees the name and the link succeeds. The next
  `capture.py` run kills the stale instance itself — `prepare()` calls
  `H.kill_all()` before it launches anything.
- **Anything checked once, at startup, will be checked at the wrong moment.**
  Three separate bugs (§7.7, §7.12, §7.15). If a resource might not exist yet,
  retry.
- **A threshold chosen from one observation becomes "never".** Five times now:
  the id probe judging at 8 leased slots when its own guard needs 16; `marked >=
  100` as "in gameplay" when the *menu* marks 106; a sim-running test accepting
  +3 objects out of 564,553; slot eviction firing with slots free; and the
  ground-truth evictor exemption below.
- **A number that looks stable is a number nobody is writing.** Every run
  produced exactly 61 masks; the cap was two stale marker files, not the constant
  I kept raising. "My fix had no effect" is a stop signal.
- **Marker files outlive the run that created them.** `tools/reset_markers.ps1`
  is the single authoritative list and every runner calls it first. Adding a
  marker to `dllmain.cpp` means adding it there, once.
- **A filter that can hide evidence needs a log line upstream of itself.**
  Happened twice, months apart (§2.4, §7.3).
- **Counters that only go up measure effort, not result.** `marked 250 this
  batch`, `255 live slots, 0 evictions`, `21 masks captured` were all true and
  all describing failures.
- **Direct-from-the-engine is not the same as correct.**
  `UGameplayStatics::IsGamePaused` authoritatively answers the wrong question: it
  reports the *engine* pause a popup sets, while inZOI runs its own world clock.
  It reads false while the world is frozen.
- **Look at the screen.** Hours of theorising about pause coordinates and
  injected-input filtering ended when one screenshot showed the harness had been
  clicking a **loading screen** the whole time.
- **The screensaver switches the input desktop** after 60s idle and no window can
  be focused from `Default`. Handled, but if focus fails again print
  `InputDesktop()` before theorising.
- **Windows does not flush a file's mtime while a handle is open and appending.**
  Use `st_size` to decide whether a log is advancing; `st_mtime` reported healthy
  games as dead and killed two runs.

---

## If there is more time

- **Root-cause the two crash families.** The highest-value open item; it is the
  only thing standing between "retries around it" and "does not happen".
- **Crop the HUD** out of captured colour frames, or copy before the UI pass.
- **Split `dllmain.cpp`.** 1,243 lines doing marker parsing, thread management
  and world probing — three responsibilities in one file. Same for the `Hooks`
  class, which holds election, probe, capture and ring state behind one
  lifetime. Neither is a bug; both are the first thing a reader trips on.
  (`IsDerivedFrom("MeshComponent")` used to be listed here. It is **done** —
  `IsRenderableComponent` walks the class hierarchy and the name list is only an
  additional accept.)
- **Continuous capture** rather than a fixed budget, for real dataset collection.
- **`UFunction` call histogram** from the ProcessEvent hook — the game telling
  itself what is happening. Cheap, and a genuinely interesting artifact.

`docs/evidence/ab-diff-result.txt`:

```txt
noise floor -- the game's own frame-to-frame variation
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
off vs off (baseline)        max=  1  mean= 0.043  p99=  1  differing=  112690 (12.228%)
on vs on                     max=  2  mean= 0.043  p99=  1  differing=  111831 (12.134%)

the actual question -- marking off vs marking on
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
off vs on                    max=  2  mean= 0.045  p99=  1  differing=  116801 (12.674%)

verdict
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
noise floor (mean) : 0.043
off-vs-on   (mean) : 0.045
ratio              : 1.04x the noise floor

PASS: enabling CustomDepth marking does not change the rendered image
      beyond the game's own frame-to-frame variation.

Method
------
Single run, static camera (menu navigation only, no patrol), A/B capture mode.
Marking took effect at frame 8031; frames 7560/7680 are before it and 8280/8400
after, all from the same session so animation phase, streaming state and TAA
history are continuous across the comparison.

Two separate runs were rejected as a design: across sessions the cat's idle
animation and the NPCs sit at different phases, which produces a large pixel
difference that has nothing to do with CustomDepth.

The noise floor is not a formality. With a completely static camera, 12.2% of
pixels still differ between two captures because Stray uses temporal AA and
jitters the sample pattern every frame. Against a threshold of zero this test
would report a visual change on every comparison regardless of what we did.

`docs/evidence/stray-groundtruth-pass.log`:

```log
Stray ground-truth intervention -- PASS

Unmark exactly one primitive's bRenderCustomDepth via the engine's own
setter, and require exactly that id's pixels to disappear from the mask.
This is the only check in the project that cannot be satisfied by
coherent-but-wrong data: every other one reads the buffer and asks whether
it looks right, this one CHANGES the world and requires the mask to follow.

Companion to inzoi-groundtruth-pass.log. That one proves it on UE5.6 +
Nanite, where the ids live in a separate R16G16_UINT colour target. This
one proves the same property on UE4, where they live in the depth-stencil's
stencil plane -- a different engine, a different carrier, the same test.

Note the direction of the second number. The OTHER slots GAIN pixels, they
do not merely stay still, and that is the correct signature rather than a
tolerance being met: the unmarked surface stops writing to CustomDepth, so
it stops occluding there, and whatever is behind it paints through its
silhouette. A mask that simply blanked the slot would leave the rest
unchanged.

Run: capture.py stray --seconds 120 --groundtruth   (2026-08-13)
Full log archived under captures/stray_20260813_212631/

<header class="top">
  <p class="eyebrow">Take-home · originlab.ai · build log</p>
  <h1>Per-pixel object IDs from a shipped game, start to finish</h1>
  <p class="standfirst">
    The complete construction record for <strong>segcap</strong> — an injected DLL that
    extracts a segmentation map from <em>Stray</em> while it runs. Written as a
    chronology: every step gets what it was for, why that approach, how it was built, and
    what it measured. Every failure gets its symptom, its real cause, and what it cost.
  </p>
  <p class="byline">
    <span>Stray · UE4 · D3D12 · retail Steam build</span>
    <span>55 commits</span>
    <span>6,579 lines C++ · 3,972 lines tooling</span>
    <span>~35 documented failures</span>
  </p>
</header>
